name: Linear Search
summary: Finds a value by checking every item in turn. Works on any list in any order, and takes time proportional to the length of the list.
simple: Linear search is the plainest way to find something: look at every item, one after another, until you see the one you want. Think of hunting for one sock in a drawer full of loose socks. You pick up a sock and check it. If it is the wrong one, you pick up the next. You stop when you find your sock, or when the drawer is empty. A computer does the same with a list. It starts at the first item and asks: is this the one? If not, it moves to the next item. If it reaches the end without a match, it reports that the item is not there. The method always works, and the list can be in any order. Its weakness is speed. A list twice as long can take twice as many checks. That is fine for a short list. It is too slow for a huge list that gets searched again and again.

analogy.title: A name on an unsorted sign-up sheet
analogy.text: Someone hands you a sign-up sheet where people wrote their names in the order they arrived. To find out whether Priya signed up, you put your finger on the first line and read down, one name at a time. You stop at her name if you see it. If your finger reaches the bottom of the sheet, you know she is not on it.
analogy.limits: Your eye can take in several lines at a glance and may catch a familiar name before your finger gets there. The algorithm cannot. It examines exactly one item at a time, in order, and learns nothing about the items it has not reached. A person might also remember roughly where a name was written. Linear search remembers nothing between one search and the next.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Find the number 17 in this list of six numbers: 3, 8, 12, 17, 21, 30. Positions are counted from 0, as programmers usually do, so 3 is at position 0 and 30 is at position 5.
whatFollows.takeaway: Check every item in turn until you find the one you want or run out of items.

name: Binary Search
summary: Finds a value in a sorted list by checking the middle item and discarding the half that cannot contain it, repeating until the value is found or nothing is left.
simple: Binary search finds an item in a sorted list by cutting the list in half again and again. You already know the idea. To find a word in a paper dictionary, you do not start at page one. You open the book near the middle and look at a word. If your word comes later in the alphabet, you can ignore the whole first half. If it comes earlier, you can ignore the second half. Then you do the same with the half that is left. Each look throws away half of the remaining pages, so the pile shrinks very fast. A list of a thousand items needs about ten looks. A list of a million needs only about twenty. There is one firm condition: the list must already be in order. If it is not, a look at the middle tells you nothing about which half to keep, and the method can give wrong answers.

analogy.title: The higher-or-lower guessing game
analogy.text: A friend picks a whole number from 1 to 100 and answers each guess with "higher", "lower" or "correct". Guess 50. If the answer is "higher", the number is somewhere from 51 to 100, so guess the middle of that range. Keep guessing the middle of whatever range is left. Each answer removes half of the remaining numbers, and seven guesses are always enough, whatever number was picked.
analogy.limits: In the game the number is always there. A list might not contain the target, so the search must also notice when the range has shrunk to nothing. The game also uses every number from 1 to 100 with no gaps. A real list has gaps, so binary search halves the range of positions, not the range of values, and looks at whatever value sits in the middle position. Last, your friend can answer about any guess at once. A computer needs to be able to jump straight to any position, which an array allows and a chain of linked items does not.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Find the number 16 in this sorted list of seven numbers: 2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38. Positions are counted from 0, so 2 is at position 0 and 38 is at position 6.
whatFollows.takeaway: Look at the middle of a sorted list, throw away the half that cannot hold what you want, and repeat with the half that is left.

name: Bubble Sort
summary: Sorts by repeatedly swapping neighbours that are out of order. Simple to follow and quadratic in general, but it finishes in one pass on a list that is already sorted.
simple: Bubble sort is a way to put a list in order, such as arranging numbers from smallest to largest. It may be the simplest method there is. Look at the first two items. If they are in the wrong order, swap them. Then look at the second and third items and do the same. Keep going until you reach the end of the list. That is one pass. During a pass, the biggest item gets carried all the way to the end, a little like a bubble rising to the top of a glass. Now make another pass, and the next biggest item settles beside it. Repeat until a whole pass goes by without a single swap. That means every item is in order with its neighbour, so the list is sorted. Bubble sort is easy to follow but slow on long lists. People learn it first, and then learn why other methods are faster.

analogy.title: A row of people trading places by height
analogy.text: People stand in a row in any order. Starting at the left, each person compares heights with the neighbour on their right, and the two trade places if the taller one is on the left. One walk along the row carries the tallest person all the way to the right-hand end. A second walk carries the next tallest to stand beside them. When a whole walk happens with nobody trading places, the row is in height order.
analogy.limits: In a real row, many pairs could trade places at the same moment, and anyone can glance along the row and see who is badly out of place. Bubble sort checks one pair at a time and never looks further than the next neighbour. The picture also hides how uneven the method is: a tall person at the left is carried to the right in a single pass, but a short person at the right moves only one place to the left per pass.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Sort the five numbers 5, 1, 4, 2, 8 from smallest to largest. A pass means walking through the list from the left, comparing each number with its right-hand neighbour.
whatFollows.takeaway: Keep swapping neighbours that are in the wrong order, and stop when a whole pass needs no swaps.

name: Selection Sort
summary: Sorts by repeatedly finding the smallest remaining value and swapping it into place. Always n(n − 1)/2 comparisons, but never more than n − 1 swaps.
simple: Selection sort is a way to put a list in order, such as arranging numbers from smallest to largest. It works the way many people tidy a shelf. Look through the whole list and find the smallest item. Move it to the front by trading places with whatever was there. That first spot is now finished. Next, look through the rest of the list and find the smallest item that is left. Trade it into the second spot. Keep going, one spot at a time, until every spot holds the right item. To find the smallest item, the method checks every remaining item in turn and remembers the smallest it has seen so far. It does all of that checking even when the list was already in order, so it is slow on long lists. Its strength is that it moves items very rarely: at most one trade for each spot.

analogy.title: Lining up books by height
analogy.text: To arrange a shelf of books from shortest to tallest, run your finger along the whole shelf and find the shortest book. Swap it with the book at the left-hand end. Then run your finger along the rest of the shelf, find the shortest of those, and swap it into the second place. Each sweep fixes one more book, and no book that has been fixed is ever touched again.
analogy.limits: A person can spot the shortest book on a shelf at a glance. A computer cannot glance: it has to look at every remaining book, one at a time, remembering the shortest it has seen so far, and it must do so on every sweep. A person would also remember which books were nearly the shortest. Selection sort forgets everything it learned in a sweep except the one winner, and starts the next sweep from nothing.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Sort the five numbers 5, 3, 8, 1, 4 from smallest to largest. In each round, search the numbers that are not yet in place for the smallest one, by comparing each with the smallest seen so far.
whatFollows.takeaway: Find the smallest item that is left, swap it into the next free spot, and repeat.

name: Insertion Sort
summary: Sorts by inserting each value into place among those already in order. Quadratic in general, close to linear on nearly sorted input, and the finisher inside hybrid sorts.
simple: Insertion sort is a way to put a list in order, and it is how most people sort a hand of playing cards. Pick up the cards one at a time. The first card is in order by itself. Take the second card and put it before or after the first, whichever is right. Take the third card and slide it into the right place among the first two. Carry on like this. Each new card goes into its correct place among the cards you already hold, so the cards in your hand are always in order. When there are no cards left to pick up, the whole hand is sorted. This method is quick when the list is short. It is very quick when the list is almost in order already, because each item is then close to where it belongs. On a long, jumbled list it is slow, because items have to travel a long way.

analogy.title: Sorting a hand of cards
analogy.text: You hold a few cards in your left hand, already in order. You pick up one more card with your right hand, look along the held cards from the right until you find one that is not larger, and slide the new card in just after it. Your left hand is in order again, with one more card. Repeat until the table is empty.
analogy.limits: With real cards, opening a gap is a single motion of the fingers. In a list stored in a computer, there is no free space between items: every larger value has to be copied one place to the right, one at a time, and that copying is where most of the time goes. A person also finds the place at a glance, while the algorithm compares one card after another.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Sort the five numbers 5, 2, 4, 6, 1 from smallest to largest. The first number, 5, starts as an ordered group of one. Each step takes the next number, called the key, and inserts it into the group.
whatFollows.takeaway: Take each item in turn and slide it left into its place among the items already in order.

name: Merge Sort
summary: Sorts by splitting the list in half, sorting each half, and merging the two sorted halves. Stable, guaranteed O(n log n), at the cost of O(n) extra memory.
simple: Merge sort is a way to put a list in order by splitting one big job into smaller jobs. It rests on one easy trick. Suppose you have two piles of cards, and each pile is already in order. You can combine them into a single ordered pile quickly. Look at the top card of each pile, take the smaller one, and repeat until both piles are gone. That is called merging. Merge sort uses this trick again and again. Cut the list in half. Cut each half in half, and keep cutting until every piece is a single item. A single item is already in order. Now merge the pieces in pairs to make ordered pieces of two. Merge those to make ordered pieces of four, and carry on until one ordered list remains. Merge sort does about the same amount of work whatever order the list starts in, so no input can catch it out.

analogy.title: Two sorted stacks of exam papers
analogy.text: Two teachers each hold a stack of exam papers sorted by student name. To combine them, they look at the top paper of each stack, move whichever name comes first onto a new stack, and repeat. Nobody ever looks below the top of a stack, and the new stack comes out fully sorted. If the original stacks were not sorted, each teacher could split theirs in two, hand the halves to helpers, and merge what comes back.
analogy.limits: The desk in this picture has room for a third stack. A computer has to set that room aside: merge sort needs spare memory as large as the list it is sorting. The helpers in the picture also work at the same time, while the algorithm on this page finishes one half completely before it starts the other. And the picture stops at a few helpers, where the algorithm keeps splitting all the way down to single papers.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Sort the four numbers 5, 2, 4, 1 from smallest to largest. To merge two ordered groups, compare their front numbers and take the smaller, until both groups are used up.
whatFollows.takeaway: Split the list in half, sort each half the same way, then merge the two sorted halves by always taking the smaller front item.

name: Quick Sort
summary: Sorts by partitioning around a pivot, then sorting each side. Fast in practice, in place, and quadratic only when pivots are chosen badly.
simple: Quick sort is a way to put a list in order, like sorting a hand of playing cards from lowest to highest. It works by picking one item from the list and asking the same question of every other item: are you smaller or bigger than this one? Smaller items go to one side. Bigger items go to the other side. The item you picked is now sitting in exactly the right spot, and it never has to move again. Then you do the same thing inside each side. The groups keep getting smaller until each one holds a single item. At that point the whole list is in order. Computers sort lists all day long: names, prices, scores, search results. Quick sort matters because, on most lists, it gets the job done with very little work.

analogy.title: Sorting a class by height with one volunteer
analogy.text: Ask one student to stand still. Everyone shorter moves to their left, everyone taller to their right. That student is now standing in exactly the right place in the final line, even though neither group is sorted yet. Repeat inside each group with a new volunteer, and keep going until every group is a single person.
analogy.limits: A class can shuffle around all at once, with everyone checking their height against the volunteer at the same moment. A computer running quick sort checks one item at a time. That is why we measure its work by counting comparisons. The picture also hides a risk: if the volunteer happens to be the shortest or tallest person every time, each round sorts out only one person, and the whole thing becomes slow.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Sort the five numbers 4, 7, 2, 9, 5. In each group, use the last number as the pivot. The pivot is the item that everything else in the group is compared against.
whatFollows.takeaway: Pick one item, put everything smaller on its left and everything bigger on its right, then do the same to each side.

name: Heap Sort
summary: Sorts by arranging the array as a max-heap, then repeatedly moving the largest value to the end and repairing the heap. In place, with a guaranteed O(n log n).
simple: Heap sort is a way to put a list in order by picking out the biggest item again and again. Finding the biggest item in a jumbled list is slow, because you have to look at every item. Heap sort avoids that by first arranging the items in a pattern called a heap. Picture a chart like a family tree. One item sits at the top, two sit below it, two below each of those, and so on. The rule is that every item is at least as big as the two items directly below it. With that rule, the biggest item is always at the top. Heap sort takes the top item and puts it at the back of the list, where it belongs. Then it repairs the chart, which takes only a few steps, because only one path from top to bottom needs fixing. Now the next biggest item is at the top. Take it, repair, and repeat until nothing is left.

analogy.title: Finding the runner-up in a knockout tournament
analogy.text: After a knockout tournament everyone knows the champion. To find the second-best player there is no need to play the whole tournament again: the runner-up must be someone the champion beat, and that is only one player per round. A heap works in a similar way. Once the largest value has been taken from the top, only the values along a single path from top to bottom need to be compared to find the next largest. For a thousand values that is about ten levels, not a thousand checks.
analogy.limits: A tournament bracket writes every player at the bottom and copies winners upward, so names appear several times. A heap stores each value once and promises less: only that a parent is at least as large as its children. Two values on different branches are in no known order. A heap also needs no bracket drawn anywhere. It is just the list itself, read with a rule that says which positions count as children of which.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Sort the five numbers 4, 10, 3, 5, 1. Read the list as a tree: 4 is at the top, 10 and 3 are its children, and 5 and 1 are the children of 10. A heap is an arrangement in which every parent is at least as large as its children.
whatFollows.takeaway: Arrange the list so the largest item is always on top, then keep taking the top item and repairing the arrangement.

name: Counting Sort
summary: Sorts whole-number keys by counting how often each occurs and computing every position directly. Linear time when the key range is small; wasteful when it is large.
simple: Counting sort puts a list in order without asking which of two items is bigger. It works when the items are whole numbers from a small range, such as exam marks from 0 to 100. Imagine sorting a big pile of exam papers by mark. Draw a tally chart with one row for each possible mark. Go through the pile once and add a tally for each paper. Now you know how many papers got each mark. From that you can work out where every group belongs in the finished pile. If three papers scored 0 and five scored 1, then the papers that scored 2 must start at the ninth place. Go through the pile a second time and put each paper straight into its place. This is very fast when the range of marks is small. It is wasteful when the range is huge, because the chart needs a row for every possible value, whether or not any paper has it.

analogy.title: Pigeonholes in a sorting office
analogy.text: A sorting office has a wall of pigeonholes, one for each delivery district, arranged in order. A clerk picks up each letter, reads its district number, and drops it into that pigeonhole. No letter is ever held up against another letter. When the sack is empty, walking along the wall from the first hole to the last collects the letters in district order.
analogy.limits: A pigeonhole can hold any number of letters, but a block of computer memory cannot stretch. That is why counting sort makes a counting pass first: it has to know how much room each key needs before it writes anything. The picture also depends on the wall being a sensible size. A hole for each of a hundred districts is fine. A hole for every possible phone number would fill the building with empty holes, and walking past them all would take longer than sorting the letters any other way.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Sort the six numbers 3, 1, 3, 2, 1, 3. The number an item is sorted by is called its key. Here the keys run from 1 to 3, so three counters are enough. Positions in the output are numbered from 0, as computers number them.
whatFollows.takeaway: Count how many of each value there are, work out where each group starts, and put every item straight into its place.

name: Hash Table with Linear Probing
summary: Stores keys in an array at positions computed from the keys themselves. On a collision it tries the next slot along. Lookups take expected constant time while the table is not too full.
simple: A hash table stores things so that you can find any one of them almost at once, without searching through the rest. Think of a cloakroom with a row of numbered hooks. When you hand in a coat, the attendant uses a fixed rule to turn your ticket number into a hook number, and hangs the coat there. When you come back, the same rule gives the same hook, so the attendant walks straight to it. Sometimes the rule sends two tickets to the same hook. The version in this lesson handles that simply: if the hook is taken, try the next hook along, then the next, until one is free. To find a coat later, start at its hook and walk along in the same way until you see it. If you reach an empty hook first, the coat is not there. This works well while plenty of hooks are free. As the rack fills, taken hooks bunch together and the walks get longer.

analogy.title: Assigned parking on a ring road
analogy.text: Every resident of a circular street has an assigned parking space worked out from their house number. If someone else is already in your space, you drive on and take the next free one. To find a neighbour's car, go to their assigned space and walk forward from there. You will reach the car before you reach a gap, because when they parked there was no gap before the space they took.
analogy.limits: On a real street cars drive away and leave gaps. In the table a gap means "stop looking", so a key that is removed must leave a marker behind, or keys parked beyond it would be lost. A person can also glance down the street and spot a car from a distance. The computer checks one slot at a time. And a house number says nothing about where a hash function will send it: a good hash function scatters keys so that similar keys land far apart.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: A table has 10 slots, numbered 0 to 9. The rule for choosing a slot is: take the last digit of the key. That slot is the key's home slot. Store the keys 23, 47, 13, 87 and 33, in that order. Each look at a slot is called a probe.
whatFollows.takeaway: Work out from the key itself where it should go, and if that place is taken, use the next free one along.

name: Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union)
summary: Tracks which items belong to the same group as groups merge. Each group is a tree named by its root; two simple rules keep the trees almost flat.
simple: Union-find keeps track of which things belong to the same group while groups keep merging. Picture a school where friend circles form over time. At first every student is alone. Whenever two students become friends, their two circles join into one. At any moment you may want to ask: are these two students in the same circle? Union-find answers that quickly. Each circle has one member who acts as its captain. Every other student remembers just one person in the circle, someone a step closer to the captain. To find your captain, you ask that person, who asks theirs, and so on, until the chain reaches the captain. Two students are in the same circle exactly when they reach the same captain. To merge two circles, one captain simply starts pointing to the other. Two small habits keep these chains short, so even with millions of students each question takes only a few steps.

analogy.title: Companies that keep merging
analogy.text: Every employee knows one thing: who their boss is. The one person with no boss is the chief executive, and the chief executive identifies the company. To learn which company someone works for, ask their boss, then that boss's boss, until you reach a chief executive. Two people work for the same company exactly when this leads to the same person. When two companies merge, one chief executive starts reporting to the other, and in that single change everyone below them has joined the bigger company.
analogy.limits: In a real company the chain of bosses means something. Here the links are bookkeeping and nothing else: who points to whom says nothing about the items except which group they are in. That is why the structure is free to rearrange itself, pointing everyone it passes straight at the top, which no real organisation would do. Real companies can also split up again. Union-find cannot undo a merge.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: There are six items, numbered 0 to 5. Each starts in a set of its own and is its own parent, so each is a root. Every root also keeps a number called its rank, which starts at 0 and is a limit on how tall its tree can be. Use both rules: the root with the smaller rank goes underneath, and a find repoints what it passes.
whatFollows.takeaway: Give every group one leader, have every member point toward that leader, and merge two groups by pointing one leader at the other.

name: Breadth-First Search
summary: Explores a graph outward from a start node one layer at a time, which finds the route with the fewest edges to every node it can reach.
simple: Breadth-first search is a way to explore a network of connected things, one layer at a time. Think of a rumour spreading through a school. On day one, a single student knows it. On day two, all of that student's friends know. On day three, the friends of those friends know, and so on. Breadth-first search explores in the same order. It starts at one point. It visits everything one step away, then everything two steps away, then three. To keep that order straight, it uses a waiting line. Each newly found point joins the back of the line, and the next point to explore always comes from the front. Because it works outward in layers, the first time it reaches a point, it has found a route there with the fewest possible steps. That is why it can find the shortest way through a maze, or the smallest number of introductions that connect two people.

analogy.title: Ripples from a stone dropped in a pond
analogy.text: Drop a stone into still water and a ring spreads outward. The ring reaches nearby points first and distant points later, and it never skips ahead. Breadth-first search spreads through a network the same way. The first ring is every node one edge from the start, the second ring is every node two edges away, and each ring is finished before the next begins.
analogy.limits: A ripple touches every point on a ring at the same moment. The algorithm visits one node at a time, so it needs the queue to remember whose turn is next. A ripple also travels real distance, while the search only counts steps: a long road and a short road each count as one. When the lengths matter, the picture is still right but the algorithm must change to Dijkstra's.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Five places are joined by paths: A to B, A to C, B to D, C to D, and D to E. Starting from A, find the fewest paths you must walk to reach each place. Neighbours are checked in alphabetical order.
whatFollows.takeaway: Explore everything one step away before anything two steps away, and the first route you find to each place is a shortest one.

name: Depth-First Search
summary: Explores a graph by following one route as far as it goes, then backing up to the most recent node that still has an untried edge.
simple: Depth-first search is a way to explore a network of connected places. It follows one route as far as it goes before trying another. Think of exploring a maze. You walk forward, and at every junction you take a passage you have not tried yet. You keep going until you reach a dead end or a place you have already been. Then you walk back to the last junction that still has an untried passage, and take it. To avoid going round in circles, you mark each place the first time you step into it. To find your way back, you remember the route you came by. When you have backed all the way out to the start and no untried passage is left, you have visited every place that can be reached. Computers use this method to solve puzzles, to find loops in a network, and to work out which jobs must be done before others.

analogy.title: Exploring a maze with a ball of string
analogy.text: Tie one end of a string at the entrance and unwind it as you walk. Put a chalk mark on every junction you enter. At each junction, take any passage whose far end is unmarked. When every passage leads somewhere marked, wind the string back to the previous junction and try again from there. The string is the stack: it always traces the route from the entrance to where you stand. The chalk marks are the record of discovered nodes.
analogy.limits: A person in a maze can see down a corridor and guess which way looks promising. The algorithm has no such sense: it tries passages in whatever order they are listed. The string shows a way back to the entrance, not the shortest way. A place right next to the entrance may be reached only at the end of a long winding route. And a walker spends real effort winding the string back, while the computer returns to the previous junction in one step.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Five places are joined by paths: A to B, A to C, B to D, C to D, and D to E. Start at A and try neighbours in alphabetical order. Keep a list of the places on your current route, in order. That list is called the stack.
whatFollows.takeaway: Go as far as you can along one route, and when you are stuck, step back to the last place that still had an untried way out.

name: Topological Sort (Kahn's Algorithm)
summary: Orders the nodes of a directed graph so that every arrow points forward, by repeatedly taking a node that nothing else is waiting on. Reports a cycle if no order exists.
simple: Topological sorting puts a set of jobs in an order that obeys every "this before that" rule. Think of getting dressed. Socks go on before shoes. Trousers go on before a belt. A shirt goes on before a jacket. No single rule gives you the whole order, but together they forbid many orders. Here is a way to find one that works. Look for a job that is waiting for nothing, and do it. Cross off every rule that starts with that job. Some other jobs may now be waiting for nothing, so they are ready too. Keep doing a ready job and crossing off its rules until every job is done. If you get stuck with jobs left over, the rules must go round in a circle, such as A before B and B before A. Then no order can work. Computers use this method to decide which files to build first and which spreadsheet cells to calculate first.

analogy.title: Choosing courses with prerequisites
analogy.text: A course catalogue lists which courses must be passed before others. To plan a degree, first write down any course with no prerequisites. Having "taken" it, cross it off the prerequisite lists of every other course. Some courses now have nothing left on their lists, so they become available. Keep picking an available course until the plan is complete. If two courses each list the other as a prerequisite, neither ever becomes available, and the catalogue has a mistake.
analogy.limits: A student can take several courses in the same term. The algorithm writes one line, a single course at a time, and when several are available it picks by an arbitrary rule. So the order it returns is one valid order among possibly many, and it says nothing about how to finish in the fewest terms. Real prerequisites can also be waived or satisfied in alternative ways. The algorithm treats every arrow as absolute.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Baking a cake takes five jobs. B: buy the ingredients. H: heat the oven. M: mix the batter. O: bake it in the oven. I: ice the cake. Four rules apply: B before M, M before O, H before O, and O before I. Find an order for the jobs.
whatFollows.takeaway: Keep doing a job that is waiting for nothing, and if you get stuck with jobs left over, the rules contradict each other.

name: Dijkstra's Algorithm
summary: Finds the cheapest route from one node to every other node of a graph with non-negative edge weights by always expanding the closest unsettled node.
simple: Dijkstra's algorithm finds the cheapest way to get from one place to every other place on a map. Picture towns joined by roads, where each road has a cost, such as minutes of driving. You start at home, which costs nothing to reach. Then you look for the nearest town you have not finished with. Nothing closer is left, so you already know the cheapest way to get there. Mark that town as finished. Next, check each road leading out of it. If going through this town gives a cheaper way to reach a neighbour, write down the new, lower cost. Now repeat: pick the nearest unfinished town, finish it, update its neighbours. When every town is finished, you know the cheapest cost to reach each one, and the route that gets you there. Phones use this idea to plan journeys. The internet uses it to decide where to send data.

analogy.title: Water spreading through pipes
analogy.text: Pour water into the source node of a network of pipes whose lengths equal the edge weights. The water front reaches each junction at a time equal to its shortest distance from the source, and it reaches junctions in order of that distance. Dijkstra's algorithm simulates the front: the priority queue always knows which junction the water will touch next.
analogy.limits: Real water flows down every pipe at once. The algorithm deals with one junction at a time, so it needs a waiting list to tell it which junction comes next. The picture also assumes every pipe has a real length. A road with a negative cost has no meaning for water, and it breaks the algorithm too.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Four towns are joined by roads. A to B costs 4. A to C costs 1. C to B costs 2. B to D costs 5. Find the cheapest cost from A to every town.
whatFollows.takeaway: Always finish the nearest unfinished place next, and use it to improve your best guesses for its neighbours.

name: Bellman-Ford Algorithm
summary: Finds cheapest routes from one node by sweeping over every edge up to V − 1 times. Slower than Dijkstra, but it allows negative weights and detects negative cycles.
simple: The Bellman-Ford algorithm finds the cheapest route from one place to every other place on a map. It still works when some roads have a negative cost, meaning that travelling the road earns you something back. Picture a delivery driver. Most roads cost fuel, but one road has a paying job on it. The method is patient. Write zero next to the start and "unknown" next to every other place. Then go through the whole list of roads. For each road, ask one question: does taking this road reach its far end more cheaply than the best known so far? If it does, write down the lower cost. One sweep through the list is not enough, because a new low cost in one place can lead to new low costs further on. So sweep again, until a whole sweep changes nothing. If the costs never stop falling, some loop of roads pays you every time you drive round it. Then no cheapest route exists, and the method says so.

analogy.title: Towns passing on news of a cheaper route
analogy.text: Every town keeps a signpost showing the cheapest known cost of reaching it from the capital. Once a day, each town tells its neighbours: "you can be reached through me for my cost plus the road between us." A town that hears a better offer than its signpost shows repaints the sign. News of a cheap route spreads one road further each day. If the map has V towns, any sensible route uses at most V − 1 roads, so after V − 1 days every signpost is right.
analogy.limits: In the story every town speaks at the same moment, and news moves exactly one road per day. The algorithm on this page checks roads one at a time in a fixed order and uses each new number immediately, so in one pass good news can travel along several roads if they happen to be listed in a helpful order. That is why it often finishes early. The story also has no ending when a loop of roads pays out: the towns would repaint their signs for ever. The algorithm stops after V − 1 passes and uses one more scan to detect the loop.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Four towns are joined by one-way roads. A to C costs 2. C to D costs 1. A to B costs 5. B to C costs −4: this road pays you 4 instead of charging you. Find the cheapest cost from A to every town. Check the roads in the order just listed, and keep making passes until nothing changes.
whatFollows.takeaway: Check every road again and again, taking any improvement on offer, until a whole round changes nothing.

name: A* Search
summary: Finds a cheapest path to a goal by always exploring the position with the lowest total of cost so far plus estimated cost to go.
simple: A* (say "A star") is a way to find the shortest route to a goal without wasting time searching in the wrong directions. Imagine crossing a city on foot toward a tall tower you can see in the distance. At every street corner you could ask two things. How far have I walked to get here? And how far does it still look to the tower? Add the two numbers, and you have a guess at the length of a whole trip through that corner. A* keeps a list of corners it could explore next, and it always picks the one with the smallest total. Corners that lead away from the tower get large totals, so they wait at the bottom of the list. Many are never explored at all. If the "how far does it look" guess never says the goal is farther than it really is, the route A* finds is truly the shortest. Video games use it to move characters, and robots use it to plan their paths.

analogy.title: Walking toward a landmark you can see
analogy.text: You are crossing an unfamiliar town toward a tower visible above the rooftops. The straight-line distance to the tower is an estimate of how far you still have to go. Streets may force detours, so the real walk is at least that long, never shorter. At each corner, the distance walked so far plus the straight-line distance remaining is the best case for any route through that corner. A* always continues from the corner with the best such total.
analogy.limits: A walker stands in one place and must walk back to try a different street. A* does not walk. It keeps a list of every corner it could continue from and jumps to whichever is most promising, at no cost. The picture also assumes your eye judges the distance correctly. If your estimate is too high, A* may settle for a route that is not the shortest. And if you cannot see the tower at all, the estimate is useless and A* has to search in every direction.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: A robot stands on a grid of squares. The goal is 5 squares to its right, with nothing in the way. The robot can step up, down, left or right. Give each square a score made of two numbers: the steps taken to reach it, and the steps that would remain if nothing were in the way (count the squares across plus the squares up or down). Always explore the unexplored square with the lowest score.
whatFollows.takeaway: Always explore the place where steps taken plus a careful guess of steps remaining is smallest, and you reach the goal by a shortest path without searching everywhere.

name: Minimax with Alpha-Beta Pruning
summary: Chooses a move in a two-player game by assuming the opponent always replies as well as possible, and skips branches that provably cannot change the choice.
simple: Minimax is how a computer chooses a move in a game for two players, such as noughts and crosses or chess. It looks ahead. It imagines each move it could make, then each reply the other player could make, then its own answers to those, and so on. At the end of every imagined line of play it writes down a score: high if the game went well for the computer, low if it went badly. Then it works backwards. On its own turns it assumes it will pick the move with the highest score. On the other player's turns it assumes they will pick the move with the lowest score, the one that is worst for the computer. The move that still comes out best is the one it plays. There is also a shortcut, called alpha-beta pruning. Once one reply shows that a move is worse than a move already found, the computer stops looking at that move. Its other replies no longer matter. The shortcut never changes the answer. It only saves work.

analogy.title: Choose a bag, and a rival picks what you get from it
analogy.text: Three bags sit on a table. You choose a bag, and then a rival, who wants you to get as little as possible, takes one thing out of it and hands it to you. To choose well you look into each bag and find its worst item, because that is the one you will be given. Then you take the bag whose worst item is best. That is minimax. Now the shortcut. Say the worst thing in the first bag is worth 4. You open the second bag and the first thing you see is worth 2. You can close that bag at once. Your rival would hand you that item or something worse, and you already have a bag that guarantees 4. Whatever else is in the second bag makes no difference.
analogy.limits: A bag is one choice deep. A game goes many turns deep, with you and your rival choosing in turn, so each item in a bag is itself a bag, and a limit found near the top of the tree is carried down to cut branches far below. The picture also assumes your rival always picks what is worst for you. A real opponent makes mistakes, and minimax does nothing to tempt them into one. And in a large game nobody can look into every bag: the search has to stop early and estimate.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Two players, Max and Min. Max wants a high score and Min wants a low one. Max is at position A and can move to B, C or D. Then Min chooses one of three endings, and each ending has a score. Under B the endings score 4, 7 and 5. Under C they score 2, 9 and 8. Under D they score 6, 3 and 1. Which move should Max make?
whatFollows.takeaway: Assume your opponent will always make the reply that is worst for you, choose the move whose worst case is best, and stop studying a move as soon as one reply proves it worse than a move you already have.

name: Q-Learning
summary: Learns how good each action is in each situation by trying actions, seeing the reward, and nudging a table of values toward what it has just experienced.
simple: Q-learning is a way for a computer to learn what to do by trying things and seeing what happens. Nobody tells it the rules. Picture a robot in a room it has never seen. Somewhere there is a prize, and somewhere a hole it can fall into. The robot keeps a notebook. For every spot in the room, and every direction it could step from that spot, the notebook holds one number: its guess at how well things will turn out if it steps that way. At first every guess is zero. The robot wanders. When a step wins the prize, it raises the number for that step. When a step lands in the hole, it lowers it. And here is what makes it work. When a step only leads to a spot that already has a good number, part of that goodness is copied back to the step. So good numbers spread, one step at a time, from the prize back to the start. In the end the robot follows the biggest number from each spot. Now and then it still tries a random step, in case a better way exists.

analogy.title: Signposts in a park with no map
analogy.text: You walk in a large park with no map, looking for the café. At every junction stands a signpost with one blank space for each path. The first time a path brings you straight to the café, you write a high number in that path's space. Later you arrive at an earlier junction and take a path that leads to a junction whose best number is already high. You write a slightly lower number for the path that got you there. Walk after walk, the numbers spread outward from the café. In the end, from any junction, you can reach the café by following the highest number on each signpost.
analogy.limits: A person would remember the whole walk and start to picture the map. Q-learning remembers nothing except the numbers, and after each step it changes only the one number for the step just taken, using only the next signpost. That is why it is slow: one walk moves what has been learned back by a single junction. The picture also hides the gamble at every junction, between following the best number and trying a path whose number is low or blank, which is the only way to find out that a signpost is wrong. And a park stays put. If the same path could lead to different places on different days, each number would have to become an average over many tries.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: A robot is in a short corridor: cell B, then cell C, then the goal. Reaching the goal gives a reward of 10. Every other step gives 0. The robot keeps one number for the move "right" in each cell, its guess at how good that move is. Both numbers start at 0. After each step it moves one number halfway toward a target. The target is the reward it just got, plus 0.9 times the best number in the cell it arrived in. (The 0.9 says that a reward one step away is worth a little less than a reward in hand.)
whatFollows.takeaway: After every step, nudge your guess for that step toward the reward you got plus the best you now expect from where you landed, and good guesses will spread back from the reward.

name: Kruskal's Algorithm
summary: Builds the cheapest set of edges that connects every node, by taking edges from lightest to heaviest and skipping any that would close a cycle.
simple: Kruskal's algorithm finds the cheapest way to connect a set of places so that you can get from any one of them to any other. Imagine several villages with no roads between them. An engineer has a list of roads that could be built, each with a price. The villages want everyone to be able to reach everyone else, for the least money in total. The method is short. Sort the list from the cheapest road to the most expensive. Go down the list one road at a time. If a road joins two villages that cannot yet reach each other, build it. If they can already reach each other, even by a roundabout route, skip it, because it would cost money and connect nothing new. Stop when all the villages are linked. The surprise is that this works. Always taking the cheapest useful road, with no planning ahead, gives the cheapest possible network.

analogy.title: Islands and bridges
analogy.text: Picture a group of islands and a price list of bridges that could be built between pairs of them. Build the cheapest bridge first. Two islands joined by a bridge count as one landmass from then on. Keep taking the next cheapest bridge on the list. If it would join two different landmasses, build it. If both of its ends are on the same landmass, it is a waste of money, so cross it off. When only one landmass is left, you are done.
analogy.limits: The network this produces is the cheapest to build, not the most convenient to travel. Two neighbouring islands may end up connected only by a long route through several others. The picture also hides how the algorithm knows whether two islands are on the same landmass. Checking that quickly, many thousands of times, needs a data structure of its own, called union-find. And real engineers can do things the list does not allow, such as building a junction in open water. The algorithm only chooses among the edges it is given.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Four villages, A, B, C and D, need to be connected. Five roads could be built: A to B for 1, B to C for 2, A to C for 3, C to D for 4, and A to D for 5. Find the cheapest set of roads that links all four.
whatFollows.takeaway: Take the cheapest connection that joins two things not yet joined, again and again, and you get the cheapest way to connect everything.

name: PageRank
summary: Scores each node of a directed graph by how much rank flows into it from the nodes that link to it, repeating the calculation until the scores stop changing.
simple: PageRank is a way to measure how important each page is in a web of pages that link to one another. It was created to help a search engine decide which results to show first. The idea is that a link is a kind of vote. A page that many others link to is probably worth reading. But the votes are not equal. A link from an important page counts for more than a link from a page nobody visits. That sounds like a circle: to score one page, you need the scores of the others. The way out is to start by giving every page the same score. Then let each page share its score out along its links, and repeat. After enough rounds the scores stop changing. Another way to picture it is a bored reader who clicks links at random for ever, and now and then jumps to a random page. A page's score is the share of time that reader spends on it.

analogy.title: The random surfer
analogy.text: Imagine someone browsing with no purpose at all. On each page they usually click one of its links, chosen at random. Now and then, with a fixed probability, they get bored and jump to a page picked at random from the whole web. Follow this surfer for a very long time and count the visits. The share of time spent on each page is its PageRank. Pages with many links pointing at them are visited often, and so are pages linked from those.
analogy.limits: Real readers do not click at random. They read, search, follow some links far more than others, and use bookmarks. PageRank is not a measurement of traffic. It is a score computed from the links alone, and it knows nothing about what a page says or whether it is any good. The random jump is not a claim about behaviour either. It is there for a mathematical reason: without it, dead ends and closed loops of pages would trap the surfer, and the scores would not settle to a single sensible answer.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Three web pages link to each other. A links to B and to C. B links to C. C links to A. Imagine 120 people browsing, 40 on each page. Every minute, half the people on each page click one of its links, split evenly between the links. The other half get bored and jump to a page chosen at random, so of the 60 people who jump, 20 land on each page.
whatFollows.takeaway: A page is important if important pages link to it, and you can find every page's score by sharing scores along the links again and again until they stop changing.

name: Critical Path Method
summary: Finds the shortest possible length of a project and the tasks that cannot run late, with one forward and one backward sweep over tasks linked by dependencies.
simple: The critical path method works out how long a project must take and which jobs cannot be late. A project is a set of jobs, and some jobs have to wait for others. You cannot paint a wall before it is built. Jobs that do not wait for each other can be done at the same time by different people. So a project is usually much shorter than all of its jobs added together. What matters are the chains of jobs that must happen one after another. The longest chain sets the length of the whole project. It is called the critical path. If any job on it runs a day late, the whole project ends a day late. Jobs that are not on it have spare time, called slack. They can start a little late and nothing bad happens. Knowing this tells the person in charge where to watch closely and where there is room to breathe.

analogy.title: Cooking a dinner with several dishes
analogy.text: A roast needs 20 minutes of preparation and then 100 minutes in the oven. The vegetables need 10 minutes of chopping and 20 minutes of cooking. A sauce takes 15 minutes. Everything should be ready together. Dinner cannot be served sooner than 120 minutes after you begin, because the two steps of the roast must follow one another and together they take that long. That chain is the critical path. The vegetables and the sauce can each be started at any moment inside a wide window, and dinner is still on time. Start the roast five minutes late, and dinner is five minutes late.
analogy.limits: One cook has two hands. The method assumes that tasks which do not wait for each other can always run at the same time, as if there were enough cooks and burners for everything. It also treats every time as known exactly, while real tasks run over. And it only describes the plan you gave it. It does not say how to make the project shorter.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Building a garden shed takes six tasks. Lay the base: 3 days. Wait for the windows to be delivered: 6 days. Build the walls: 4 days, after the base. Fit the windows: 1 day, after the walls are up and the windows have arrived. Put on the roof: 2 days, after the walls. Paint: 2 days, after the windows are fitted and the roof is on. Tasks that do not wait for each other can run at the same time. Count time in days from the start, so the project begins at day 0.
whatFollows.takeaway: A project is as long as its longest chain of tasks that must follow one another, and only the tasks on that chain have no time to spare.

name: Fibonacci by Dynamic Programming
summary: Computes Fibonacci numbers three ways to show the central move of dynamic programming: solve each subproblem once, store the answer, and reuse it.
simple: Dynamic programming is a way to stop a computer doing the same work twice. The Fibonacci numbers make a good first example. They start 0, 1, and after that each number is the sum of the two before it: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. Suppose you want the thirtieth one. One way is to say: I need the two numbers before it. For each of those, I need the two before them, and so on down. That works, but it asks for the same small answers again and again, millions of times in all. A better way is to keep a notebook. The first time you work out an answer, write it down. The next time you need it, read it from the page. Better still, start from the small end and fill the page in order. Now about thirty short sums are enough. The same habit, solving each small problem once and reusing the answer, speeds up many harder problems.

analogy.title: A notebook of answers
analogy.text: A pupil is asked the same long sum several times in one lesson. The first time, they work it out and write the answer in a notebook. Every later time, they read it off the page. The work is done once however often the question comes back. Bottom-up dynamic programming goes one step further: knowing which questions will come, the pupil works through them in order, easiest first, so that every answer needed is already on the page.
analogy.limits: A notebook only helps when the same question really does come back, and when its answer cannot change between askings. It also takes up space: the page has one line for every different question. And the notebook does not make any single sum faster. For very large Fibonacci numbers the sums themselves become long, and no amount of remembering changes that.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: The Fibonacci numbers start 0, 1. After that, each one is the sum of the two before it: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. Count positions from zero, so the number at position 6 is 8. Here are three ways to find it.
whatFollows.takeaway: If the same small question keeps coming back, answer it once, write the answer down, and look it up from then on.

name: Longest Common Subsequence
summary: Finds the longest sequence of characters that appears in two strings in the same order, by filling a table over all pairs of prefixes and tracing back.
simple: The longest common subsequence is the longest list of letters that appears in two pieces of text in the same order. The letters do not have to sit next to each other. Take STONE and LONGEST. Cross out letters from each word until what is left is the same in both. The most you can keep is ONE. That shared part is what the two texts have in common, and everything outside it is what changed. This is how a computer shows the difference between two versions of a document. It finds the lines that both versions share, in order, and marks the rest as removed or added. Trying every way of crossing out letters would take far too long. So the method fills in a grid. Each square answers the question for the first few letters of each word, using the answers in the squares beside it. The last square gives the answer for the whole words.

analogy.title: Two playlists with songs in common
analogy.text: Two friends each have a playlist. They want to listen together to as many songs as possible, playing them in an order that respects both lists. Each may skip songs, but neither may go backwards. The longest such run of shared songs is the longest common subsequence of the two playlists. The songs skipped on one list are deletions, and the songs skipped on the other are insertions.
analogy.limits: A playlist rarely contains the same song twice, and without repeats the problem is easier. Text repeats letters constantly, and each copy could be paired with any copy in the other string. The choice matters, because pairing one letter rules out pairings that would cross it. That is why the table is needed. Also, there is often more than one longest common subsequence, and the algorithm reports just one of them.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Find the longest common subsequence of TEA and EAT: the longest list of letters found in both words in the same order, not necessarily side by side. Draw a grid with T, E, A down the side and E, A, T along the top. Add an extra row and column of zeros at the start for "no letters yet". Each square will hold the length of the longest shared list for the letters so far.
whatFollows.takeaway: What two texts share, in order, is found by comparing all their beginnings first: on a match extend the shared part by one, otherwise carry forward the better of two smaller answers.

name: Edit Distance (Levenshtein)
summary: Counts the fewest single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions that turn one string into another, by filling a table over all pairs of prefixes.
simple: Edit distance measures how different two pieces of text are. It counts the fewest small changes needed to turn one into the other. A small change means adding one letter, removing one letter, or swapping one letter for another. To turn CAT into CART you add an R, so the distance is 1. Spelling checkers use this idea. When you mistype a word, they look for real words that are only a change or two away from what you typed. Finding the fewest changes sounds hard, because there are so many ways to edit a word. The method here avoids trying them all. It starts with the easiest questions, about the first letter or two of each word. Then it works up to longer and longer beginnings of the two words, writing each answer in a grid. Each new answer needs only three answers already in the grid. The last square filled in is the distance between the whole words.

analogy.title: Crossing a city grid with tolls
analogy.text: Picture a grid of streets. You start at the top-left corner and must reach the bottom-right. Moving one block down means deleting a letter. Moving one block right means inserting a letter. Both cost one coin. You can also cut diagonally across a block: that is free if the two letters at that block match, and costs one coin if they differ. The edit distance is the fewest coins for the whole trip. The cheapest way to reach any corner is the cheapest of the three ways to arrive there, from above, from the left, or diagonally, so you can work out every corner in turn by sweeping across the grid.
analogy.limits: In this city every street is one-way: down, right, or diagonally down and right. That is why one sweep, row by row, is enough. On a real map with two-way streets you would need a method such as Dijkstra's algorithm. The picture also makes every toll one coin. Real typing errors are not all equally likely, and plain edit distance does not know that.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Turn the word TEA into the word EAT. One edit deletes a letter, inserts a letter, or swaps one letter for another. Draw a grid with T, E, A down the side and E, A, T along the top. Add one extra row and one extra column at the start for "no letters yet". Each square will hold the fewest edits to turn the letters down the side so far into the letters along the top so far.
whatFollows.takeaway: To compare two words, compare all their beginnings first, shortest to longest, and build each answer from the three answers just before it.

name: 0/1 Knapsack
summary: Chooses the most valuable set of whole items that fits a weight limit, by filling a table over items and capacities and tracing back the choices.
simple: The knapsack problem is about choosing what to take when you cannot take everything. Picture a hiker with a bag that can hold only so much weight. Each thing she could pack has a weight and a value to her. Which things should go in the bag so that the total value is as high as possible and the bag is not too heavy? Each item is either taken whole or left behind. That is what the 0/1 in the name means. One tempting plan is to grab the items that give the most value for their weight. That plan can fail, because it may leave space that nothing else fits. Trying every possible selection always works, but the number of selections doubles with each extra item. The method here is smarter. It builds a grid of small questions: what is the best I can do with only the first few items and a smaller bag? Each answer comes from two answers already in the grid, one for leaving the newest item and one for taking it.

analogy.title: A packing notebook for every bag size
analogy.text: Suppose you kept a notebook that says, for every bag size up to yours, the best load you could make from the items looked at so far. A new item arrives. For each bag size you now have an easy question. Leave the item, and the notebook's old answer stands. Take it, and you get its value plus the notebook's answer for the smaller bag that has room for everything else. Write down the better of the two. After the last item, the entry for your real bag is the answer.
analogy.limits: The notebook has one line per bag size, so it only works when weights are whole numbers and the capacity is not enormous. Real packing also involves shape and volume, and real items interact: a tent is worth little without its poles. The knapsack problem assumes one number for weight, one for value, and values that simply add up.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: A bag can carry 5 kilograms. There are three items: a ring (1 kg, worth 6 coins), a vase (2 kg, worth 10) and a clock (3 kg, worth 12). Each is taken whole or left behind. Make a grid with a row for each item and a column for each bag size from 0 to 5 kg. A square holds the best total value for that bag size using the items in its row and the rows above.
whatFollows.takeaway: For each item ask one question, take it or leave it, and answer that question for every bag size using the answers already worked out for the items before it.

name: Needleman-Wunsch Alignment
summary: Finds the highest-scoring end-to-end alignment of two sequences, given scores for matches, mismatches and gaps, by filling a table and tracing back.
simple: Needleman-Wunsch lines up two sequences of letters so that as many letters as possible match. Biologists use it to compare DNA or proteins from different living things. DNA can be written as a long string of four letters: A, C, G and T. Over millions of years, copies of the same gene drift apart. A letter changes here. A few letters go missing there. To see what two versions still share, you write one above the other and slide parts along, leaving gaps where letters were lost. Each matching pair of letters earns points. Each mismatched pair and each gap costs points. The best line-up is the one with the highest total. There are far too many line-ups to try them all. So the method fills in a grid. It works out the best score for the first few letters of each sequence, then for a few more, until the last square holds the best score for the whole thing. Walking back through the grid shows the line-up itself.

analogy.title: Two worn copies of the same manuscript
analogy.text: Two scribes copied the same text by hand, generations apart. Words were changed and whole lines were dropped. To compare the copies, you lay them side by side and slide lines down, leaving a blank wherever one copy seems to have lost something, until as much as possible sits next to its counterpart. A line next to an identical line is good. A line next to a different one is suspicious. A blank is a loss. The best arrangement is the one that needs the fewest suspicious pairs and blanks.
analogy.limits: A scholar comparing manuscripts uses meaning and judgement. The algorithm only adds up fixed scores, and the alignment with the best score is not guaranteed to be what actually happened. It also insists on lining up both sequences from the first letter to the last. If only a passage is shared, forcing the rest into line gives a misleading picture. And the simple scoring used here charges every gap position the same, although in real sequences one long gap is more plausible than several scattered short ones.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Line up GAT against GT. A matching pair of letters scores +1. A mismatched pair scores −1. A letter opposite a gap scores −1. Draw a grid with G, A, T down the side and G, T along the top, plus an extra row and column at the start for "no letters yet". Each square will hold the best score for lining up the letters so far.
whatFollows.takeaway: Score every way two sequences can begin, shortest beginnings first, and the best line-up of the whole sequences falls out of the last square of the grid.

name: Binomial Option Pricing
summary: Values an option by building a tree of possible share prices and working backwards from the payoffs at expiry, node by node. A teaching model, not advice.
simple: An option is a ticket that lets you buy or sell something later, such as a share in a company, at a price fixed today. You may use the ticket or throw it away. Suppose a ticket lets you sell a share for 100 a year from now. If the share is then worth 80, the ticket gains you 20. If the share is worth 120, the ticket is useless and you ignore it. So what should the ticket cost today, when nobody knows the future price? This method draws a tree. From today's price the share can step up or step down. From each of those prices it can step up or down again, and so on until the last day. On the last day the ticket's worth is easy to see at every branch tip. Then you work backwards. The worth at each fork is a careful blend of the two worths that follow it. Fork by fork you arrive back at today, and the number you reach is the price of the ticket. It is the answer of a simplified model, not a promise about any real market.

analogy.title: Labelling a trail map from the ends back to the start
analogy.text: Imagine a trail that forks again and again, with a prize of known size at the end of every branch. You stand at the start and want to know what the walk is worth. Looking forward is confusing, because there are so many routes. Looking backward is easy. Write the prize at every trail end. Then go to each last fork and write a number that blends the two prizes it leads to. Then do the forks before those, and so on. When you reach the start, its number is the worth of the whole walk. If the rules let you stop at a fork and take a fixed reward instead, compare that reward with the fork's blended number and write down the larger.
analogy.limits: On a trail map the blend could be a plain average. In the model the blending weights are forced by the sizes of the up and down moves and by the interest rate, and they are nobody's forecast. The map also has tidy forks at fixed places. A real price can jump any distance at any moment, and every real trade costs something, both of which the model leaves out.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: A share costs 60 today. In each of two steps its price either doubles or halves. A call option is the right to buy the share for 60 at the end of the second step, and not before. To keep the sums easy, money in the bank earns no interest here. What is the option worth today?
whatFollows.takeaway: Write down what the option pays at every possible final price, then step backwards through the tree, blending two later values into each earlier one, until you reach today.

name: Euclidean Algorithm
summary: Finds the greatest common divisor of two whole numbers by repeatedly replacing the larger with its remainder on division by the smaller, until the remainder is zero.
simple: The Euclidean algorithm finds the largest number that divides two whole numbers exactly. That number is called their greatest common divisor. Here is a way to picture it. A floor is 48 units long and 18 units wide. You want to cover it with identical square tiles, as large as possible, without cutting any. What size should the tiles be? Start by laying the biggest squares the floor allows, 18 by 18. Two of them fit, and a strip 12 wide is left over. Now treat the strip the same way. One 12 by 12 square fits, and a smaller strip 6 wide is left. Squares of side 6 fill that last strip exactly, with nothing left. So 6 is the answer: tiles of 6 by 6 cover the whole floor. The method is more than two thousand years old. It is still in daily use, for example when computers create the keys that keep messages private.

analogy.title: Measuring two sticks against each other
analogy.text: You have a long stick and a short stick and want the longest ruler that measures both exactly. Lay the short stick along the long one as many times as it fits and mark what is left over. Any ruler that measures both sticks must measure that leftover piece too. So forget the long stick: the problem is now the short stick and the leftover. Repeat with those two. When a piece fits with nothing left over, that piece is the ruler.
analogy.limits: With real sticks the process might never end. The side and the diagonal of a square have no common measure at all, and the leftovers get smaller forever. The algorithm is about whole numbers, where each leftover is a smaller whole number and so the process must stop. The picture also suggests laying the stick down one length at a time, which is repeated subtraction. The algorithm does all of those subtractions at once with a single division.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Find the greatest common divisor of 48 and 18: the largest whole number that divides both. Dividing one number by another gives a quotient (how many times it fits) and a remainder (what is left over).
whatFollows.takeaway: Divide the larger number by the smaller, keep the smaller number and the remainder, and repeat until the remainder is zero.

name: Sieve of Eratosthenes
summary: Finds every prime up to a limit by writing out the numbers and crossing out the multiples of each prime in turn. Whatever is never crossed out is prime.
simple: The sieve of Eratosthenes finds all the prime numbers up to a limit you choose. A prime is a whole number bigger than 1 that cannot be divided evenly by anything except 1 and itself, such as 2, 3, 5 and 7. A kitchen sieve keeps what you want by letting everything else fall away, and this method does the same with numbers. Write down every number from 2 up to your limit. The first number, 2, is prime. Cross out every multiple of 2 after it: 4, 6, 8 and so on. Now move to the next number that is not crossed out. That is 3, so 3 is prime. Cross out its multiples. Keep going. Each time, the next number still standing is prime, and its multiples get crossed out. When you finish, the numbers left are exactly the primes. Nothing ever has to be divided. You only count along the list in equal steps.

analogy.title: Children sitting down in a line
analogy.text: Children wearing the numbers 2 to 100 stand in a line. The first child, number 2, stays standing and walks down the line asking every second child after them to sit: 4, 6, 8 and so on. Then the next child still standing, number 3, asks every third child after them to sit. Then number 5 does the same with every fifth child. When nobody new is left to take a turn, the children still standing are wearing exactly the prime numbers.
analogy.limits: Some children are asked to sit more than once: number 12 hears it from 2 and again from 3. The computer wastes effort in the same way, and it is the main inefficiency of the method. The picture also needs one child for every number up to the limit. That is the real cost of the sieve: memory for the whole range. It is fine for a limit of a hundred or a hundred million, and impossible for numbers with hundreds of digits.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Find every prime up to 30. A prime is a whole number above 1 whose only divisors are 1 and itself. Write the numbers 2 to 30 in a row and cross numbers out as you go.
whatFollows.takeaway: Write down the numbers, and each time you reach one that has not been crossed out, call it prime and cross out all its multiples.

name: Fast Modular Exponentiation
summary: Computes a power modulo m using the binary digits of the exponent: square for every digit, multiply once more for every 1. The work grows with the length of the exponent, not its size.
simple: Fast modular exponentiation finds the remainder of a huge power without ever working out the huge power. Suppose you multiply 1,000 sevens together and want the remainder when the result is divided by 13. The full product has more than 800 digits. You do not need it. Two ideas get the answer using small numbers only. First, you may take the remainder after every multiplication and carry on from there. The final remainder comes out the same, and no number ever grows beyond 13 times 13. Second, you do not need 1,000 multiplications. Squaring a result doubles the count of sevens multiplied into it: 2, then 4, then 8, then 16. By mixing squarings with a few extra multiplications by 7, you can land on exactly 1,000 in fewer than twenty steps. The encryption that protects messages and payments online depends on this, using numbers hundreds of digits long.

analogy.title: A copier that can only double
analogy.text: You need a stack of exactly 13 sheets. Your machine has two buttons. One doubles the whole stack. The other adds a single sheet. Starting from 1 sheet: double and add one to get 3, double to get 6, double and add one to get 13. Four steps of doubling, with an extra sheet twice, instead of adding one sheet twelve times. Which steps get the extra sheet is not a guess. It is read off 13 written in binary, 1101: after the leading 1, each digit means "double", and each 1 means "then add one".
analogy.limits: The stack counts how many copies of the base have been multiplied together, which is the exponent, not the value of the power. Doubling the stack corresponds to squaring the running result, and adding a sheet corresponds to multiplying by the base once. The picture also leaves out the other half of the method: taking the remainder after every step, which is what keeps the numbers small.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Find the remainder when 5 to the power 13 is divided by 23. "To the power 13" means 13 copies of 5 multiplied together. In binary, 13 is written 1101, because 13 = 8 + 4 + 1. Keep a running result, and after every multiplication replace it by its remainder on division by 23.
whatFollows.takeaway: To raise a number to a big power, read the exponent in binary: square for every digit, multiply once more for every 1, and keep only the remainder as you go.

name: Bisection Method
summary: Solves f(x) = 0 by trapping a sign change between two points and halving that interval until it is as narrow as required.
simple: The bisection method finds the exact spot where something changes from too little to too much. Think of a shower dial. At one setting the water is too cold. At another setting it is too hot. Somewhere between the two is the setting that is just right. So you try the setting exactly halfway between. If the water is still too cold, the right setting must be in the upper half. If it is too hot, the right setting must be in the lower half. Either way, the gap you have to search is now half as wide. Try the middle of that gap, and halve it again. After ten tries the gap is about a thousand times narrower than at the start. After twenty tries it is a million times narrower. Computers use this to solve equations that no formula can solve. It is not the fastest method, but it is the safest. As long as the thing being measured changes smoothly, the answer can never slip out of the gap.

analogy.title: Finding the right setting on a dial
analogy.text: A shower dial is too cold at one mark and too hot at another. The comfortable setting lies between them. Turn the dial to the halfway mark and feel the water. Whichever way it is wrong tells you which half holds the right setting, and you can forget the other half for good. Each test halves the stretch of dial that is still in question.
analogy.limits: A person at a shower uses more than "too hot" or "too cold". If the water is only slightly too cold, they nudge the dial a little instead of going to the halfway mark. Bisection ignores how far off the midpoint is and looks only at the sign, which is why faster methods exist. The dial also has one right setting, while a function can cross zero several times inside a bracket. Bisection then finds one of the crossings and says nothing about the others.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Find the number that gives 2 when multiplied by itself (the square root of 2). Call the guess x and look at x × x − 2. We want the x that makes this zero. At x = 1 it is −1, which is too low. At x = 2 it is 2, which is too high. So the answer is trapped between 1 and 2.
whatFollows.takeaway: Trap the answer between a guess that is too low and one that is too high, test the middle, keep the half that still traps it, and repeat.

name: Newton's Method
summary: Solves f(x) = 0 by following the tangent line at the current guess to where it crosses zero, and repeating from there.
simple: Newton's method solves an equation by making a guess and then improving it, quickly. Suppose you want an oven at exactly 200 degrees, and the dial has no numbers. You pick a position and wait. The oven settles at 180 degrees, which is 20 too low. You also know that, around this position, one notch of the dial adds about 10 degrees. So you turn it up 2 notches. That would be perfect if every notch added exactly 10 degrees. Real dials are not that regular, so you might land on 199. You measure again and make a much smaller correction. Each round uses two facts: how far off you are, and how quickly the result changes when the guess changes. Dividing the first by the second gives the correction. Once the guess is close, every round roughly doubles the number of correct digits, so a few rounds are enough. The catch is that a poor first guess can send the method the wrong way.

analogy.title: A straight ramp laid along the curve
analogy.text: Stand on the curve at your current guess. Lay a long straight plank so that it touches the curve under your feet and points the way the curve is heading. Walk along the plank to the point where it reaches ground level, the height zero. Then step straight up or down onto the curve again and lay a new plank. If the curve is nearly straight between you and the root, the first plank almost gets you there, and the second is aimed from much closer.
analogy.limits: A plank is straight and the curve is not. If the curve bends sharply between where you stand and the root, the plank can point to a place farther away than where you started. If the curve is level under your feet, the plank is level too and never reaches the ground. And the picture hides the price: to lay the plank you must know the slope, which means having a formula for the derivative or computing an estimate of it.
