whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Find the number that gives 2 when multiplied by itself (the square root of 2). Call the guess x and look at x × x − 2, which we want to be zero. For this expression, the slope at any x is 2 × x. The slope says how fast the value changes as x changes. Start from the guess x = 1.
whatFollows.takeaway: Measure how far off your guess is and how fast things change there, divide one by the other to get the correction, and repeat.

name: Euler's Method
summary: Follows a differential equation forward in time by assuming, for each small step, that the current rate of change stays constant.
simple: Euler's method predicts the future one small step at a time. Suppose you know two things about a cup of hot tea: how warm it is now, and how fast it is cooling at this moment. What will its temperature be in one minute? A simple guess is to pretend the cooling rate stays the same for that minute. Multiply the rate by one minute and take that much off. Now you have a new temperature. Cooler tea cools more slowly, so you work out the new rate and repeat for the next minute. Step by step, you trace out the whole future of the tea. Many things in nature are like this. We know the rule for how fast they change, but there is no formula for where they end up. Planets, populations and electric circuits are examples. The smaller the steps, the closer the prediction stays to the truth, and the more steps it takes. With steps that are too big, the prediction can go badly wrong.

analogy.title: Navigating with only a compass and a speedometer
analogy.text: A ship out of sight of land cannot see where it is. The navigator knows the last marked position, the heading and the speed. So for the next hour the navigator draws a straight line on the chart in that direction, as long as the distance the ship would cover in an hour, and marks a new position at its end. Then the instruments are read again and the next line is drawn. The plotted course is a chain of straight segments standing in for the curved path of the real ship.
analogy.limits: The ship's instruments measure the real ship, wherever it truly is. Euler's method computes the rate of change from its own estimated position. Once the estimate has drifted, the rates it uses belong to the wrong place, so errors can feed on themselves. A navigator also sights land sooner or later and corrects the chart. Euler's method never receives a correction: every error it makes is carried forward to the end.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: A quantity starts at 1 and always shrinks at a rate equal to its own size. When it is 1, it is falling at a rate of 1 per unit of time. When it is 0.5, it is falling at a rate of 0.5. Predict it at times 0.5, 1, 1.5 and 2, using steps of 0.5.
whatFollows.takeaway: Assume the current rate of change holds for one short step, take the step, then measure the rate again.

name: Runge-Kutta (RK4)
summary: Advances a differential equation one time step by sampling the slope four times within the step and following their weighted average.
simple: Runge-Kutta is a careful way to predict the future one step at a time. Suppose you want to know where a rolling ball will be one second from now. The quick way is to check its speed now and pretend that speed holds for the whole second. But the ball may be slowing down, so the quick guess goes too far. The careful way takes four readings of the speed instead of one. The first is the speed right now. The second is the speed the ball would have half a second from now, if the first reading were right. The third is the speed at the half second again, using the second reading to get there. The fourth is the speed at the end of the second. Then the method averages the four, counting the two middle readings twice, and moves the ball by that average. Each step is four times the work. In return the answer is so much more accurate that far fewer steps are needed.

analogy.title: A navigator who checks the water ahead
analogy.text: A navigator plotting the next hour could draw one straight line using the current heading and speed. A more careful navigator first asks what the wind and current would be half an hour along that line, and redraws using those. Then checks the half-hour point again along the corrected line, then the full-hour point. The course finally drawn blends all four readings, giving most weight to the two taken at the middle of the hour.
analogy.limits: A real navigator cannot measure the sea at a place the ship has not reached. The method can make its trial readings only because the rule of change is a formula that can be evaluated for any time and any state, including states the system never visits. The weights are also not a navigator's judgement: they are fixed by algebra so that the errors of the four readings cancel as far as possible. And like Euler's method, RK4 never receives a correction from outside, so whatever error it makes is carried forward.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: A quantity starts at 1 and grows at a rate equal to its own size: when it is 1 it grows at 1 per unit of time, when it is 2 it grows at 2. Take a single step of length 1. The rate of change at any moment is called the slope. The true answer after one unit of time is 2.71828.
whatFollows.takeaway: Before each step, sample the slope at the start, twice at the middle and once at the end, then step along their weighted average.

name: Fast Fourier Transform
summary: Computes the discrete Fourier transform of n samples in O(n log n) operations by merging the transforms of the even and odd samples.
simple: A Fourier transform takes a mixed-up signal and tells you what simple ingredients it is made of. Think of a chord on a piano. Three keys are pressed together, and the three notes travel through the air as one wobbling wave. A microphone records only that one combined wave. Yet your ear can tell that three notes are in it. A Fourier transform does the same job with arithmetic. It takes the recorded wave and reports how much of each pitch it contains: a lot of this note, some of that one, none of the others. The fast Fourier transform, or FFT, is a quick way to do that arithmetic. The plain way checks the recording against every possible pitch, one at a time, which is slow. The FFT splits the recording into halves again and again, and reuses the work that different pitches have in common. For a recording of about a thousand numbers, that is roughly two hundred times less work. That speed is why phones, audio software and medical scanners can use it constantly.

analogy.title: Hearing the notes in a chord
analogy.text: When a chord is played, the air carries a single complicated vibration: the sum of the vibrations of each string. Nothing in that vibration is labelled with the names of the notes. Even so, a listener hears the separate notes, because the ear responds to each pitch on its own. A Fourier transform is the same unmixing done with numbers. It is handed the single combined wave and gives back a list: this pitch at this strength, that pitch at that strength.
analogy.limits: The ear listens continuously and judges pitch on its own scale. The FFT looks at one fixed block of samples and can only report on a fixed ladder of frequencies: 0, 1, 2, 3 and so on whole cycles per block. A note that falls between two rungs is smeared across several of them. The FFT also describes the block as a whole, so it cannot say when within the block a note began or ended. And it cannot see any frequency above half the sampling rate: such a note shows up disguised as a lower one.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Four measurements of a signal, taken one after another, are 6, 1, 4, 1. They were made by adding three simple patterns: a steady level (1, 1, 1, 1), a slow wave that rises and falls once (1, 0, −1, 0), and a fast wave that flips at every measurement (1, −1, 1, −1). How much of each pattern is in the signal?
whatFollows.takeaway: A signal is a mix of pure waves, and the FFT finds how much of each is present by splitting the samples in half again and again and reusing the shared work.

name: Gradient Descent
summary: Minimizes a differentiable function by repeatedly stepping in the direction of steepest descent, the negative gradient.
simple: Gradient descent is a way to find the lowest point of something when you cannot see all of it. Imagine standing on a hillside in thick fog. You want to reach the bottom of the valley. You cannot see the valley, but you can feel which way the ground slopes under your feet. So you take a small step downhill. Then you feel the slope again and take another step. Keep going, and you end up somewhere low. Computers use the same trick with numbers. They start with a guess. They measure how wrong the guess is, and work out which small change would make it less wrong. They make that change, then repeat, often millions of times. This is what people mean when they say a computer program is learning: each step makes its answers a little less wrong.

analogy.title: Walking downhill in fog
analogy.text: You are on a hillside in thick fog and want to reach the valley floor. You cannot see the valley, but you can feel which way the ground slopes under your feet. So you take a step in the steepest downhill direction, feel the slope again, and repeat. Your stride length is the learning rate: tiny strides are safe but slow, and giant strides can carry you clear across the valley and up the other side.
analogy.limits: A hiker moves smoothly. The algorithm jumps from point to point, and a jump that is too long can leap right over the valley floor and land higher up on the far side. A hillside also has only two directions to move in, while the problems solved in machine learning have millions of directions at once. And fog or no fog, a hiker who reaches a small dip may be nowhere near the deepest valley. The algorithm has the same weakness.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Find the lowest point of the curve y = x × x, starting from x = 4. For this curve, the slope at any point is 2 × x. Each step moves by one quarter of the slope. That fraction is called the learning rate.
whatFollows.takeaway: Feel which way is downhill, take a small step that way, and repeat.

name: Simulated Annealing
summary: Searches for a low point by a random walk that always accepts improvements and accepts worse moves with a probability that falls as a temperature is lowered.
simple: Simulated annealing is a way to search for the best answer when there are far too many possibilities to check them all. Picture a hiker in thick fog who wants the lowest point in a range of hills. A hiker who only ever walks downhill stops in the first dip they reach. A much deeper valley may lie just over the next ridge, and they will never see it. Simulated annealing lets the hiker walk uphill now and then. At each step the hiker picks a random spot nearby. If it is lower, they go there. If it is higher, they might still go, by chance. Early on they say yes to uphill steps often, so they roam widely and climb out of shallow dips. As time passes they grow stricter and say yes less and less. By the end they only walk downhill and settle into the low place they have found. The name comes from annealing: heating a metal and cooling it slowly, so that its atoms settle into an orderly pattern.

analogy.title: A marble on a shaken tray
analogy.text: Picture a tray moulded with many dents of different depths, and a marble that you want in the deepest dent without looking. If you hold the tray still, the marble rolls into the nearest dent and stays there. So you shake the tray. Hard shaking throws the marble out of any dent, shallow or deep. Then you shake more and more gently. There comes a stage where the shaking can still knock the marble out of a shallow dent but not out of a deep one, so the marble tends to collect in a deep one. When the shaking stops it rests there. The strength of the shaking is the temperature.
analogy.limits: A real marble rolls smoothly and carries momentum. The algorithm has neither: it proposes a jump, then accepts or refuses it by a rule of chance. The tray also suggests that patience always wins the deepest dent, and that is not true. With any cooling schedule fast enough to be practical, the search often ends in a good dent that is not the best one. And many real uses have no surface at all. The position is an arrangement, such as the order in which to visit cities, and a nearby point is the same arrangement with one small change.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: A walker wants the lowest of five stones in a row. Their heights are A = 6, B = 3, C = 5, D = 1 and E = 4. The walker starts on B. Both neighbours of B are higher, so a walker who only steps down stays on B for ever and never finds D. This walker follows the annealing rule instead. A step down is always taken. A step up is taken with a chance that depends on how big the rise is and on a number called the temperature. The temperature starts at 4 and halves after every step.
whatFollows.takeaway: Accept every improvement, accept some setbacks while the search is young, and grow stricter as it goes on.

name: Genetic Algorithm
summary: Improves a population of candidate solutions over generations by selecting the better ones, blending pairs of them, and applying small random changes.
simple: A genetic algorithm searches for a good answer in the way a breeder improves animals or crops. A breeder who wants faster horses does not design a horse. They let the fastest ones have foals, and they repeat that for many generations. A genetic algorithm does the same with possible answers to a problem. It starts with a crowd of random guesses. It scores every guess to see how good it is. Then it builds a new crowd. Good guesses are picked more often to be parents. Two parents are blended to make a child that takes after both. Now and then a child is changed a little at random, which brings in something new. The new crowd replaces the old one, and the cycle repeats. Over many rounds the crowd drifts toward better answers. Nobody tells it how to improve. It only needs a way to tell a better guess from a worse one. It does not promise the best answer, only a good one.

analogy.title: Selective breeding
analogy.text: A plant breeder wants wheat that survives drought. Each season they grow a field of plants, see which ones cope best, and keep seed mostly from those. They cross promising plants with each other, hoping a child inherits the strengths of both. Now and then a seed carries a small accidental change, and once in a while that change helps. The breeder never works out what a drought-proof plant should look like. They only compare plants and decide which ones get to have offspring. After enough seasons the field looks very different from the first one.
analogy.limits: The algorithm borrows three ideas from breeding and almost nothing else. Real inheritance works through genes in ways far more intricate than averaging two numbers. A breeder's field holds thousands of plants and takes a year per generation, while the algorithm uses a few dozen candidates and judges each by one fixed score. Natural evolution has no score and no goal at all. So a genetic algorithm is not a simulation of evolution, and nothing about biology guarantees that it will work on a given problem.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Find the number that makes this score as small as possible: subtract 7 from the number, then multiply the result by itself. The population has four members: 1, 4, 10 and 12. One round of the algorithm, called a generation, goes like this.
whatFollows.takeaway: Keep a crowd of guesses, let the better ones have more children, mix and slightly alter those children, and repeat.

name: Simplex Method
summary: Maximises a linear objective under linear limits by walking from corner to corner of the allowed region, raising the objective at each step, until no neighbouring corner is better.
simple: The simplex method finds the best mix of things to make when several limits apply at once. Picture a bakery that sells bread and cakes. Cakes earn more money. But there are only so many cake tins, so much oven space and so many hours in the day. Every possible plan is a point on a map: so much bread across, so many cakes up. Each limit rules out part of the map with a straight line. What is left is a shape with flat sides and corners. Here is the key fact. If there is a best plan, one of the corners is a best plan. So there is no need to check the endless points inside the shape. The method starts at the corner where nothing is made. It looks along the edges that leave that corner and follows one that raises the profit. At the next corner it does the same again. When no edge leads to more profit, it stops. That corner is the best plan.

analogy.title: Walking the fence of a sloping field
analogy.text: A farmer's field lies on an even slope and is fenced with straight runs of fence. You want to stand at its highest point. Because the ground slopes evenly, the highest point cannot be in the middle of the field or partway along a fence: wherever you stand, you could go a little higher by walking uphill until a fence stops you, and then along that fence until a post stops you. So the highest point is at a fence post. Start at any post. Two fences leave it. If one of them climbs, follow it to the next post. Repeat. When both fences at your post lead downhill, you are at the top.
analogy.limits: A field has two directions and each post has two fences. A real problem with a thousand products is a shape in a thousand dimensions, with far more corners than could ever be listed and many edges at each one. Nobody can picture that shape, and the method never does: it works on a table of numbers, and the walk is only a way to understand what the table is doing. The slope must also be perfectly even. If the profit per item changes with the amount made, the best point need not be at a corner at all.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: A bakery makes batches of bread and cakes. A batch of bread earns 2 coins and a cake earns 5. Three limits apply each day. The oven takes at most 6 batches of bread. There are only 4 cake tins, so at most 4 cakes. And there are 10 hours of work: a batch of bread takes 1 hour and a cake takes 2. How many of each should the bakery make to earn the most?
whatFollows.takeaway: When everything adds up in straight lines, a best plan sits at a corner, so walk from corner to corner along edges that raise the profit until none does.

name: Stochastic Gradient Descent
summary: Gradient descent that estimates the gradient from one example or a small random batch at each step instead of the whole dataset.
simple: Stochastic gradient descent is how a computer learns from a mountain of examples without looking at all of them before every move. Suppose a program should guess a house's price from its size, and it has a million past sales to learn from. It starts with a bad guessing rule. To improve the rule, it could check it against all million sales, work out the best small change, and make it. That is slow: a million checks for one small change. So it does something quicker. It picks a handful of sales at random, checks the rule on only those, and makes the small change they suggest. Then it picks another handful and does it again. Each handful gives a rough answer, a bit off in some random direction. But the handfuls are off in different directions, so over many steps the errors mostly cancel while the improvements add up. The word stochastic means random: chance decides which examples are used at each step.

analogy.title: Asking ten customers instead of the whole town
analogy.text: A baker wants to know whether the town would like the bread saltier or sweeter. Asking all 20,000 townspeople would give a reliable answer, once, after weeks. Instead the baker asks ten customers picked at random, changes the recipe slightly in the direction they favour, and asks ten different customers the next day. Any ten people can be unusual, so on some days the recipe moves the wrong way. Over many days the unusual groups pull in different directions and cancel, and the recipe drifts toward what the town as a whole prefers. Asking a hundred people each day gives a steadier answer, but every day then costs ten times as much.
analogy.limits: The baker adjusts one thing. A model has many adjustable numbers, and each batch gives a direction for all of them at once. The baker could also stop when the customers seem content, but the batches in this method never agree: even at the best recipe, each small group still asks for some change, so the recipe keeps jittering unless the changes are made smaller over time. Last, the picture only works if the ten are chosen at random. A baker who only asks the early morning crowd ends up with bread for early risers, and a program that forgets to shuffle its data makes the same mistake.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Four points: A (−1, −1), B (1, 1), C (−1, 0) and D (1, 0). The line starts flat, with slope 0 and height 0. The best line for these four points is known: slope 0.5, height 0. Each step looks at one point only. Find the gap, which is the point's y minus the line's y at that point. Then add a quarter of the gap to the height, and add a quarter of the gap times the point's x to the slope. The quarter comes from the learning rate, the number that sets how big each change is.
whatFollows.takeaway: Check a few random examples, take a small step the way they point, and repeat: each step is rough, but there can be a great many of them.

name: Adam Optimizer
summary: Gradient descent with memory: it steps along a running average of recent gradients and gives every parameter its own step size.
simple: Adam is a recipe for walking downhill when you can only feel the slope under your feet. Picture a hiker in fog, in a long, narrow valley. A plain walker takes big steps where the ground is steep and tiny steps where it is nearly flat. That goes badly here. The steep side walls throw the walker from side to side, while the gentle slope along the valley floor, the way that matters, earns only tiny steps. Adam adds two kinds of memory. First, it remembers which way the slope has pointed lately and steps in that averaged direction. Side-to-side slopes keep flipping, so they cancel. The slope along the valley keeps pointing the same way, so it adds up. Second, it keeps a separate memory for north-south and for east-west of how big the slopes have usually been, and divides by it. A direction with huge slopes gets its steps shrunk. A direction with tiny slopes gets its steps stretched. Computers use this recipe to train neural networks, which have millions of adjustable numbers instead of two directions.

analogy.title: A fog walker with a memory and a separate stride for each compass direction
analogy.text: A walker in fog feels the slope underfoot and wants the valley floor. This walker keeps two notebooks. The first holds a running average of recent slopes, and the walker heads the way that average points, so a slope that flips back and forth is averaged away while a slope that persists builds up. The second holds, separately for north-south and for east-west, how large the slopes have typically been. Before stepping, the walker divides by the typical size in each direction. Where the ground has been steep, the stride is shortened. Where it has been gentle, the stride is lengthened. The result is a walker who covers ground at a similar pace in both directions, whatever the steepness.
analogy.limits: No real walker can stride one length north-south and a different length east-west at the same moment. Adam can, because it treats every adjustable number on its own. That is also where the picture gives a warning: the adjustment works along the compass directions only. If the valley runs diagonally, both compass directions see the same mixture of steep and gentle slopes, and the separate strides help much less. The memory has a cost too. Carried by its averaged direction, the walker goes past the lowest point and has to turn back. And a real network has millions of directions, not two.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: A surface with two settings, x and y. Its slope in x is equal to x, and its slope in y is 100 times y, so it is far steeper in y. Start at x = −2, y = 0.2. The lowest point is at x = 0, y = 0. The learning rate, the number that sets the step length, is 0.1. Adam keeps two running averages for each setting: one of the slope, and one of the slope multiplied by itself.
whatFollows.takeaway: Step the way the recent slopes agree on, and give every adjustable number its own step size, smaller where its slopes have been large.

name: Linear Regression
summary: Fits a straight line to data by choosing the slope and intercept that make the squared vertical gaps between line and points as small as possible.
simple: Linear regression is a way to draw the best straight line through a scatter of dots. Suppose you write down how tall each of your classmates is and how big their shoes are. Put one dot on a chart for every person. The dots form a rough, sloping cloud, because taller people tend to have bigger feet. No straight line passes through every dot, so which line is the best one? The usual answer goes like this. For each dot, measure how far above or below the line it sits. Multiply each of those gaps by itself, so that big misses count for a lot. Then add them all up. The best line is the one with the smallest total. A computer can find it by starting with any line and nudging it, a little at a time, in whichever way makes the total smaller. Once you have the line, you can use it to make a sensible guess about someone new. Give it a height, and it reads off a shoe size.

analogy.title: A rod held by springs
analogy.text: Pin every data point to the chart. Attach a spring from each pin straight up or down to a stiff rod, and let go. Each spring pulls the rod toward its own pin, and a spring stretched twice as far stores four times the energy. The rod swings and slides until the pulls balance. That resting position is the least squares line: it is the position with the least total energy in the springs, and spring energy grows with the square of the stretch.
analogy.limits: The springs in this picture can only stretch straight up and down, which no real spring would do without a guide rail. The method measures vertical gaps on purpose, because it is predicting y from x. The picture also explains a weakness as well as a strength: one pin placed far from the others stretches its spring so much that it drags the whole rod toward itself. And the rod settles somewhere even when the pins follow a curve, so a resting position is no evidence that a straight line was the right shape to use.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Three points: (−1, −1), (0, 0.5) and (1, 0.5). The first number is the input x and the second is the output y. For any line, the gap between a point's real y and the line's y at that point is called a residual. Score a line by squaring each residual and adding the squares. Lower is better.
whatFollows.takeaway: The best line is the one that makes the squared gaps between the line and the points add up to the least.

name: k-Nearest Neighbours
summary: Labels a new point by majority vote among the k labelled training points closest to it. There is no training step: all the work happens at query time.
simple: k-nearest neighbours is a way to label something new by looking at the labelled things most similar to it. Imagine a map of a town where every house is marked with the football team that family supports. A new family moves in, and you want to guess their team. A sensible guess is to look at the few houses closest to theirs and see which team most of them support. That is the whole method. The letter k is just the number of neighbours you ask. Ask only one, and a single odd household can fool you. Ask five and take the majority, and the guess is steadier. Ask the whole town, and you only learn which team is most popular overall. Computers use the same idea with measurements in place of streets. A fruit can be described by its weight and its colour. Two fruits with similar numbers sit close together on a chart, and a new fruit gets the label that most of its nearest neighbours carry.

analogy.title: Asking the nearest houses
analogy.text: A new family moves into a town where every house flies the flag of the team it supports. To guess the newcomers' team, walk to the k houses nearest theirs and count the flags. Whichever team has the most flags among those k houses is your guess. You did not need a theory of why people support teams, and you did not need to study the town beforehand. You only needed the map and a way to measure distance.
analogy.limits: On a street map, distance has an obvious meaning and only two directions matter. Real data may have dozens of measurements in different units, such as grams and centimetres, and then the answer depends on how each one is scaled. With very many measurements, almost every point is far from every other, and the "nearest" neighbours are hardly nearer than the rest. The picture also hides the cost: to be sure which houses are nearest, the plain method measures the distance to every house in town, every time a new family arrives.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Six labelled points and one new point, the query, at the centre of the chart. The distance from the query to each point, measured with a ruler, is: point 1 (class 1) at 0.5, point 2 (class 0) at 0.6, point 3 (class 0) at 0.8, point 4 (class 1) at 1.0, point 5 (class 1) at 1.3 and point 6 (class 0) at 1.5. Use k = 3, which means the three nearest points get a vote.
whatFollows.takeaway: To label something new, find the few known examples most like it and go with the majority.

name: k-Means Clustering
summary: Splits unlabelled points into k groups by alternating two steps: give each point to its nearest centre, then move each centre to the mean of its points.
simple: k-means is a way to sort things into groups when nobody has told you what the groups are. Imagine a town that wants to put up three notice boards, so that everyone lives close to one of them. Where should they go? Start by putting the boards anywhere. Each household then picks the board nearest to it, which splits the town into three groups. Now move each board to the middle of the group that picked it. Some households will find that a different board has become their nearest, so they switch. Move the boards again, and keep going. After a few rounds nobody switches, and you stop. The boards now mark the centres of three neighbourhoods. Computers do the same with any kind of measurement, not only positions on a map. They can group customers with similar shopping habits, or the colours in a photograph. The letter k stands for the number of groups, and you have to choose it yourself.

analogy.title: Moving the notice boards
analogy.text: A town puts up k notice boards at arbitrary spots. Every household adopts the nearest board. Each board is then moved to the average location of the households that adopted it. With the boards in new places, some households find a different board is now closer, and switch. Repeat until no household switches. The boards end up in the middle of k neighbourhoods, and nobody had to define the neighbourhoods in advance.
analogy.limits: A real board cannot stand in the middle of a lake, but a centroid is a plain average and can land where there are no points at all. Households would measure distance along streets; the method uses straight-line distance and squares it, so a few far-away households pull a board strongly. The town also has to decide the number of boards before it starts, and the method will carve out that many neighbourhoods whether or not the town really has them. Finally, a bad first placement can leave two boards sharing one neighbourhood while another neighbourhood has to share a single board with its neighbour, and the procedure will not notice.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Six houses stand along a straight road at kilometre marks 1, 2, 3, 8, 9 and 10. Split them into two clusters. Start with one centre on the first house, at 1, and the other on the second house, at 2. The cost of a grouping is found by taking each house's distance to its centre, squaring it, and adding these up.
whatFollows.takeaway: Give each point to its nearest centre, move each centre to the middle of its points, and repeat until nothing changes.

name: Principal Component Analysis
summary: Finds the perpendicular directions along which data vary most, so that many overlapping measurements can be replaced by a few new ones with little lost.
simple: Principal component analysis finds the directions in which a set of measurements varies most. Suppose you measure the height and the arm span of everyone in a school. Tall pupils tend to have long arms, so the two numbers mostly rise and fall together. Plot each pupil as a dot, with height across and arm span up, and the dots form a long thin cloud running diagonally. The long way along that cloud is the first principal direction. You could call it overall size. One number, how far along the cloud a pupil sits, tells you most of what the two measurements told you. The short way across the cloud is the second direction. It holds what is left over, such as arms that are unusually long for a pupil's height. The method finds these directions by arithmetic alone. Nobody tells it what size means. It earns its keep when there are not two measurements but fifty. Often a handful of directions hold nearly all the variation, and the rest can be dropped with little lost.

analogy.title: The shadow that shows the most
analogy.text: Hold a fork between a lamp and a wall and turn it. End-on, its shadow is a small blob that could be anything. Side-on, the shadow is long and you can count the prongs. A shadow is a flattened copy of an object: three dimensions pressed into two. Principal component analysis chooses the angle that makes the shadow of a cloud of points as spread out as possible, on the grounds that the most spread-out shadow keeps the points furthest apart and so loses the least.
analogy.limits: The widest shadow is not always the one that shows what you care about. Two kinds of point can differ in a direction where the cloud is thin, and the widest shadow would press them together. A lamp also flattens three dimensions to two, while the method goes from any number of measurements to any smaller number, which no picture can show. And a cloud that is bent like a horseshoe has no flat shadow that does it justice, because the method can only choose a straight direction to look along.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Five points on a chart: (5, 4), (1, 0), (3, 2), (4, 1) and (2, 3). Think of each as two measurements of one object. The aim is to find the direction along which the five are most spread out.
whatFollows.takeaway: Find the direction along which the points spread out most, then the next one at right angles to it, and describe every point by where it sits along those few directions.

name: Logistic Regression
summary: A two-class classifier that passes a weighted sum of the inputs through an S-shaped curve to get a probability, trained by gradient descent on cross-entropy.
simple: Logistic regression is a way to answer yes-or-no questions with a probability. Think of a doctor deciding whether a patient has a certain illness, using two measurements such as temperature and heart rate. Past patients are dots on a chart: one colour for those who were ill, another for those who were not. Logistic regression draws a straight line across the chart to separate the two colours as well as it can. A new patient far on one side of the line gets a confident answer, such as nine chances in ten of being ill. A patient right on the line gets fifty-fifty. Close to the line the answer is unsure, which is honest. The computer finds the line by starting with a poor one. It checks how wrong its probabilities are for the patients it already knows about, shifts the line a little to be less wrong, and repeats. The method can only draw a straight line. If the two colours cannot be split that way, it does a poor job.

analogy.title: A ramp between a plain and a plateau
analogy.text: Picture the chart as a landscape seen from above. Along one straight line the ground is at exactly half height. On one side it rises smoothly to a plateau at height 1, and on the other it falls smoothly to a plain at height 0. The height at any spot is the model's probability that a point there belongs to class 1. Training turns the ramp, slides it and makes it steeper, until the known class 1 points stand on high ground and the known class 0 points on low ground.
analogy.limits: This ramp has the same profile all the way along, so its contour lines are straight and parallel. A real pattern may need a boundary that curves or closes on itself, which no turning or sliding of a straight ramp can produce. The height is also only the model's belief. It matches real frequencies only when a straight ramp is a fair description of the data. And if the two classes can be separated perfectly, training never finishes shaping the ramp: it keeps steepening it toward a cliff.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Four points. Two are class 0, at (−1, 0) and (0, −1). Two are class 1, at (1, 0) and (0, 1). The model has two weights and a bias, all starting at 0. A point's score is the first weight times its x, plus the second weight times its y, plus the bias. An S-shaped curve turns the score into a probability of class 1: a score of 0 becomes 0.5, a score of 1 becomes 0.73 and a score of −1 becomes 0.27. Use a learning rate of 4.
whatFollows.takeaway: Draw the straight line that best separates two groups, and let distance from the line say how sure you are.

name: Decision Tree Learning
summary: Learns a tree of yes-or-no questions from labelled examples by repeatedly choosing the split that leaves the two sides least mixed, then predicts by following the answers.
simple: A decision tree is a list of yes-or-no questions, asked in order, that ends in a prediction. Think of a phone company that wants to know which customers are about to leave. It has records of past customers: how long each had been with the company, how often each rang to complain, and whether they left. The computer looks for the single question that best sorts those records into leavers and stayers. Perhaps it is: did they complain more than twice? No question sorts perfectly, so each of the two groups gets a question of its own, and so on. Drawn on paper, the questions branch like an upside-down tree. To predict for a new customer, start at the top and follow the answers down. The path also tells you why, because the reasons are the answers along the way. There is one trap. Keep adding questions and the tree ends up memorizing the old customers, quirks and all. Then it predicts new customers worse, not better.

analogy.title: The key at the front of a field guide
analogy.text: Many field guides open with a key. Are the leaves needles or flat? If needles, do they grow in bundles? Each answer sends you to another question until you arrive at a name. A decision tree is a key of exactly that kind, with one difference: nobody wrote it. The computer built it from a pile of specimens that were already named, by choosing at each step the question that separated them best.
analogy.limits: A botanist writes a key from an understanding of plants, and it holds for every specimen of the species. A learned tree knows only the specimens it was shown, and a different pile could give a different key. The botanist can plan the whole key at once, while the tree is built one question at a time by a simple score that never looks ahead. The questions are also narrower than a botanist's: each asks whether one number is above or below a value. Finally, a key ends in a certain name. A leaf of a learned tree ends in a majority, and some of the specimens that reached it may have been something else.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: A phone company has records of eight past customers. For each it knows how many times the customer rang the help line in their last month, how many years they had been a customer, and whether they left. Four left: (5 calls, 2 years), (4, 6), (3, 4) and (1, 1). Four stayed: (0, 3), (1, 5), (2, 7) and (0, 8). To score how mixed a group is, multiply the fraction who left by the fraction who stayed, and double it. A group that is all one kind scores 0. An even mix scores 0.5, which is the highest a group can score. In the demonstration on this page, calls are x, years are y, and leaving is class 1.
whatFollows.takeaway: Keep asking the yes-or-no question that best separates the examples, stop before the questions start describing accidents, and read each prediction and its reasons off the path.

name: Perceptron
summary: Learns a straight boundary between two classes by visiting points one at a time and adjusting its weights only when it gets one wrong.
simple: A perceptron is a simple machine for sorting things into two groups, and it learns from its own mistakes. Picture a table with apples and oranges scattered across it and a ruler lying on the table. The rule is that everything on one side of the ruler is called an apple, and everything on the other side an orange. At first the ruler is in a poor position. So you check the fruit one at a time. If a fruit is on the correct side, you do nothing. If it is on the wrong side, you shift the ruler toward it, enough to give that fruit a better chance next time. Then you move on to the next fruit, and go round the table again and again. If a straight ruler can separate the fruit at all, this routine is certain to find a position that gets every one right, and then it stops. If no such position exists, it never stops fiddling. The perceptron began as a model of a single brain cell, and today's neural networks are built from units much like it.

analogy.title: Nudging a ruler across a table
analogy.text: Lay a ruler on a table covered with two kinds of fruit. Check the fruit one by one. Each time you find a fruit on the wrong side, shift and turn the ruler toward it. Do nothing for fruit that is already on the correct side. Keep going round the table until you complete a full round without touching the ruler.
analogy.limits: The ruler has no memory. A nudge that helps one fruit can push another, previously correct, onto the wrong side, which is why several rounds are needed. The size of each nudge is fixed by where the offending fruit sits, not by how wrong the ruler is. The routine stops at the first position that works, even if the ruler ends up brushing against a fruit when there was room to sit comfortably between the groups. And a ruler is straight: if the two kinds of fruit can only be separated by a curve, you will go round the table for ever.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Four points: P1 at (1, 1) is class 1, P2 at (−1, 1) is class 0, P3 at (1, −1) is class 1 and P4 at (−1, −1) is class 0. The perceptron has two weights and a bias, all starting at 0. A point's score is the first weight times its x, plus the second weight times its y, plus the bias. A positive score means class 1 and a negative score means class 0. A score of exactly 0 counts as a mistake.
whatFollows.takeaway: Check the examples one at a time, and only when you get one wrong, shift the dividing line toward it.

name: Backpropagation
summary: Computes how the loss of a neural network changes with every weight, by one forward pass and one backward pass that applies the chain rule layer by layer.
simple: Backpropagation is how a neural network finds out which of its settings to blame for a mistake. A neural network is a chain of simple calculations with many adjustable numbers, called weights. It makes a guess, and the guess is compared with the right answer. Usually the guess is somewhat wrong. The hard question is which weights to change, and by how much, when there may be millions of them. Think of a factory line where each worker passes a part to the next. A faulty product comes out at the end. The inspector tells the last worker what was wrong. That worker works out how much was their own doing and how much came from the part they were handed, and passes that message back. So it goes, worker by worker, to the start of the line. Backpropagation does this with numbers. It runs the network forwards to get the guess, then sends the error backwards, and every weight learns which way to move. The network nudges each weight a little and tries again.

analogy.title: Tracing a fault back along a production line
analogy.text: A product passes through a line of workers, each of whom does something to it and hands it on. At the end an inspector finds it is faulty and says by how much. The last worker considers how their own setting affected the product, adjusts their idea of what to do next time, and tells the worker before them how much of the fault was already in the part when it arrived. That worker does the same. The message travels back up the line, changing at each station, until everyone knows how their own setting contributed.
analogy.limits: Workers use judgment. Backpropagation uses one rule of calculus, applied mechanically, and its messages are exact rates of change that hold only for very small adjustments. In a network each unit also feeds many others, so blame comes back along many paths at once and has to be added up. And the message alone changes nothing. Deciding how far to move each setting is a separate step, done by gradient descent.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Take the smallest possible network: one input and two weights in a row. The input is 2. The first weight is 3, so the middle value is 2 × 3 = 6. The second weight is 0.5, so the output is 6 × 0.5 = 3. The right answer was 1. The loss is half the square of the miss. For each weight we want its gradient: the number that says how fast the loss grows when that weight is raised. Real networks also bend each value with a squashing function. That adds one more multiplication to each step back, and is left out here to keep the numbers easy.
whatFollows.takeaway: Run the network forwards to see how wrong it is, then pass the error backwards so every weight learns which way to move.

name: Convolution and Edge Detection
summary: Slides a small grid of weights over an image and writes one weighted sum per position. The weights decide whether the result is a blur, a sharper image or a map of the edges.
simple: A picture on a screen is a grid of tiny squares called pixels. Each pixel is stored as a number that says how bright it is. Convolution makes a new picture from an old one with the help of a small grid of numbers called a kernel. Lay the kernel over one patch of the picture. Multiply each pixel in the patch by the kernel number lying on top of it. Add up the results. That single sum becomes one pixel of the new picture. Then slide the kernel one step along and do it again, until it has visited every patch. Different kernels do different jobs. If all the kernel numbers are equal, each new pixel is an average of its neighbours, and the picture turns blurry. If one side of the kernel is negative and the other side positive, the sum is zero where the picture is smooth and large where the brightness changes suddenly. Those sudden changes are edges: the outlines of things.

analogy.title: A card with nine windows
analogy.text: Take a card with a three by three block of windows cut in it, and write a number beside each window. Lay the card on a page covered in numbers. Through each window you see one number from the page. Multiply it by the number written beside that window, add up the nine products, and write the total on a second sheet at the matching place. Slide the card one square and repeat. When the card has been everywhere, the second sheet is the filtered picture.
analogy.limits: The card makes it look like slow handwork on one patch at a time. A computer does every patch, and a real photo has millions of them. The card also hides two choices. One is what to do at the border, where the card would hang off the page. Here the card simply never goes there, so the second sheet comes out smaller. The other is whether to turn the card half a turn before using it, which is what the strict mathematical definition of convolution asks for. And a card only reports how well each patch matches its own pattern of numbers. An edge card says where brightness changes. It does not know whether the edge belongs to a face or a shadow.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: A tiny image, three rows of six pixels, is dark on the left and bright on the right. Every row reads 1, 1, 1, 9, 9, 9. The kernel is the horizontal Sobel kernel, three rows of three weights: (−1, 0, 1), then (−2, 0, 2), then (−1, 0, 1). Its left column is negative and its right column is positive, so it compares what is on its right with what is on its left. The image is three rows tall, so the kernel fits in only one row of positions, and it can stand in four places from left to right.
whatFollows.takeaway: Slide a small grid of weights across a picture and write down one weighted sum at each stop: the weights decide whether you get a blur, a sharper picture or a map of the edges.

name: Graph Neural Networks
summary: Lets every node of a graph repeatedly mix its own numbers with a summary of its neighbours' numbers, using one shared set of weights, so each round carries information one edge further.
simple: Some things are best described as a network: people and their friendships, towns and the roads between them, atoms and the bonds that hold a molecule together. A network like this is called a graph. Each thing is a node, and each link is an edge. A graph neural network is a way for a computer to work out something about each node by letting the nodes talk to their neighbours. Every node starts with a few numbers that describe it. Then comes a round of message passing. Each node collects its neighbours' numbers, averages them, and mixes that average with its own numbers by a fixed recipe. All the nodes do this at the same moment, and all of them use the same recipe. After one round a node knows something about its neighbours. After two rounds it knows something about its neighbours' neighbours, because its neighbours had already listened. The recipe contains adjustable numbers called weights. Training means trying many examples and nudging the weights until the final numbers give good answers.

analogy.title: News passed between neighbours
analogy.text: Picture a village in which each household talks only to the houses next door. Once a day, at the same hour, every household asks its neighbours what they wrote in their notebooks yesterday, averages what it hears, and writes a new entry that mixes that average with its own last entry. News from next door arrives in one day. News from two doors away takes two days, because it first has to be written into the notebook in between. After a week, each notebook reflects everything within seven houses.
analogy.limits: Villagers remember who told them what and can ask follow-up questions. A node only gets an average, so it cannot tell which neighbour said what, or even how many neighbours it has. Every household here follows the identical recipe, and the recipe is arithmetic, not judgement. Real gossip also keeps travelling for as long as people talk, while a graph neural network runs a small fixed number of rounds, so news from far away never arrives at all. And in this picture nobody chose the recipe for a purpose. In a real network the recipe is found by training.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Four nodes stand in a line, A, B, C and D, each joined to the next. Every node holds two numbers. A starts with (1, 0) and the others with (0, 0). The recipe for a round is the same for every node. The new first number is half of the node's own first number, plus half of the neighbours' average first number, minus half of their average second number. The new second number is the same with first and second swapped. Any result below zero is replaced by 0. Everyone works from the old numbers, and all the nodes switch to their new numbers together at the end of the round.
whatFollows.takeaway: Each round, every node mixes its own numbers with its neighbours' numbers by one shared recipe, so after k rounds a node knows about everything within k steps and nothing beyond.

name: Attention and the Transformer
summary: Lets every token in a sequence take a weighted blend of all the others, with weights from query-key scores. Stacked with other layers, this step forms the transformer.
simple: Attention is a way for each word in a sentence to collect information from the other words. Take the sentence: the cat sat on the mat because it was tired. To know what "it" means, you look back at "cat". A computer needs a way to do the same. In attention, every word sends out a question, and every word also wears a label saying what it has to offer. Questions, labels and everything else are lists of numbers. The computer compares one word's question with every word's label and gives each pair a score. A high score means: this word matters to that one. The scores are then turned into shares that add up to one whole, like slices of a pie. The word takes a blend of what the other words carry, with the biggest slices coming from the highest scores. Every word does this at once, so every word ends up knowing something about its sentence. A transformer is a program built by repeating this step many times, with other steps in between. The language models behind chatbots are transformers. Nobody writes their questions and labels by hand. They are found by training on enormous amounts of text.

analogy.title: A room where everyone compares notes
analogy.text: Picture a room of people, each holding three cards. The first card is a question: the kind of thing this person wants to know. The second is a badge, worn where everyone can see it, saying what this person knows about. The third is a page of notes. Each person compares their question with every badge in the room, their own included, and decides how well each badge matches. Then they collect notes from everyone, taking a large share from the people whose badges matched well and a small share from the rest. Everyone does this at the same moment, and everyone leaves with a new page that mixes what the room knew, tilted towards what they asked about.
analogy.limits: People would ask one or two others and ignore the rest. Attention takes a share from everyone it is allowed to see, and no share is ever exactly zero, only small. The cards are lists of numbers, a match is a sum of products, and nothing in the room understands anything. In a trained model no person chose the questions or the badges. They were adjusted during training, and it is often hard to say in words what a particular question is asking.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Take the five tokens "the dog saw the cat" and work out the output for one of them, "saw". A token is one item of the sequence, here a word. Each token has three lists of four numbers, set by hand for this example: a query (what it is looking for), a key (what it offers) and a value (what it hands over). The query of "saw" is 3, 0, 0, 0. The keys are: the 0, 0, 0, 1. dog 1, 0, 1, 0. saw 0, 1, 0, 0. cat 1, 0, 2, 0. The values are: the 0, 0, 1, 0. dog 2, 0, 0, 2. saw 0, 1, 0, 0. cat 3, 0, 0, 4.
whatFollows.takeaway: Each token scores every token, turns the scores into shares that add up to one, and takes that blend of what the others carry.

name: Diffusion Models (DDPM)
summary: Generates data by starting from pure noise and removing it in many small steps, using a network trained to undo a fixed, gradual noising process.
simple: A diffusion model makes pictures by learning to undo damage. Take a clear photo and sprinkle a little random speckle over it, like static on an old television. Do it again, and again. After many rounds nothing is left but static. That direction is easy and needs no cleverness. Now imagine a program that has watched this happen to millions of pictures. It learns to look at a speckled picture and guess what the clean one underneath was. To make a brand new picture, start from pure static. Ask the program for its guess, and use it to wipe away a little of the speckle. Then ask again. Step by step, shapes come out of the static. The starting static is different every time, so the finished picture is different every time. The demonstration on this page is open about one limit. Its guesser is a plain formula that knows only four tiny pictures by heart, so those four are all it can ever produce.

analogy.title: A drop of ink in water, played backwards
analogy.text: Let a drop of ink fall into a glass of water. At first it is a sharp, intricate shape. Random jostling of the water spreads it out, and after a while the glass is an even grey with no trace of the shape. Film this and play it backwards: an even grey gathers itself into a drop. A diffusion model learns what one step of that backwards film looks like. Given a slightly-too-blurry frame, it produces a slightly sharper one. Starting from plain grey and applying that step many times, it arrives at a drop.
analogy.limits: Real diffusion cannot be run backwards, and the model does not recover any particular drop that once existed. It makes up a plausible one, and a different one every time, because the grey it starts from is fresh random noise. Ink also spreads by moving through space, while the model's noise is added to each pixel separately and nothing moves. And the picture leaves out the hard part: the backwards step is not a law of nature here. It has to be learned from examples, and the result is only as good as that learning.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Shrink the problem to pictures with one pixel. The training set holds just two of them: one whose pixel is 1 and one whose pixel is −1. Pick a moment partway through the noising process at which a picture is its clean value times 0.6, plus random noise times 0.8. We noise one training picture, then ask what a perfect denoiser would say about the result.
whatFollows.takeaway: Learn to remove a little noise from a picture, then start from pure noise and remove a little, many times over.

name: Monte Carlo Estimation
summary: Estimates a quantity by drawing random samples and averaging, here the value of π from random points in a square. The error shrinks like 1/√n.
simple: Monte Carlo estimation answers a hard question by trying random cases and counting. Suppose you want to know the area of an oddly shaped pond in a square field. Measuring it directly is difficult. Instead, throw a thousand pebbles into the field without aiming, so they land everywhere equally often. Then count how many splashed. If about three in every ten pebbles hit the water, the pond covers about three tenths of the field. No geometry was needed, only counting. More pebbles give a better answer, though the improvement is slow. To get an answer ten times closer, you need about a hundred times as many pebbles. Computers are good at this, because they can produce millions of random numbers in a second. Scientists use the same trick when a problem has too many possibilities to work through one by one, such as how light bounces around a room, or what a risky investment might be worth next year.

analogy.title: An opinion poll
analogy.text: To learn what a country of millions thinks, a pollster does not ask everyone. They ask about a thousand people chosen at random and report the fraction who said yes. The answer is usually within a few percentage points of the truth, and the size of the country hardly matters: what matters is the size of the sample. Monte Carlo estimation polls the possibilities of a mathematical problem in the same way.
analogy.limits: A pollster's hard problem is reaching a fair sample of people, and people can refuse or change their minds. A computer has neither difficulty with points in a square. Its difficulties are different. Its random numbers come from a formula and only imitate chance. And for many real problems, drawing fair samples is itself hard, which is why more advanced sampling methods exist.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Estimate π from five random points. Each point has two coordinates between 0 and 1, so it lies in a square of side 1. A point is inside the quarter circle when the square of its first coordinate plus the square of its second is at most 1.
whatFollows.takeaway: When you cannot work out an answer, try many random cases and count: the fraction that succeed is your estimate, and it sharpens slowly as the cases pile up.

name: Bayesian Updating
summary: Revises a belief as evidence arrives: the new belief is the old belief reweighted by how well each possibility explains the evidence. Shown for a coin.
simple: Bayesian updating is a rule for changing your mind by the right amount when you learn something new. Imagine a friend hands you a coin and warns you it might be a trick coin. Before any flips you already have an opinion. Perhaps you think it is probably fair. Then you flip it. One head tells you very little, so your opinion should barely move. Eight heads in ten flips is harder to shrug off. Eighty heads in a hundred flips should convince almost anyone. The rule says exactly how far to shift after each flip. Start from what you believed. Ask how well each possibility explains what you just saw. Possibilities that explain it well gain strength, and the others lose strength. Two things follow. Strong evidence moves you further than weak evidence. And the more firmly you believed something at the start, the more evidence it takes to change your mind. Doctors reading test results and email filters deciding what is spam both reason this way.

analogy.title: A detective and the clues
analogy.text: A detective starts a case with some suspects more likely than others. Each clue shifts suspicion toward the suspects who would more probably have left it. Mud on the carpet points to anyone who came through the garden, a little. A fingerprint points to one person, a lot. No single ordinary clue settles the case, but they accumulate, and a suspect who started out unlikely needs stronger clues before the detective accuses them.
analogy.limits: A detective weighs clues by feel, and the rule needs numbers: how likely each suspect was at the start, and how probable each clue would be if they were guilty. Those numbers can be hard to justify, and two honest people may choose different ones. The rule also only shares belief out among the suspects on the list. If the culprit was never listed, no amount of evidence will name them.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: A coin has an unknown chance of landing heads. Start with no opinion: every chance from 0 to 1 counts as equally plausible. With that starting point, the best single guess after some flips is (heads seen + 1) divided by (flips seen + 2). The extra 1 and 2 are the starting belief, which acts like one imaginary head and one imaginary tail. The flips come up heads, heads, tails, heads.
whatFollows.takeaway: Start from what you believed, shift toward whatever explains the new evidence better, and shift further when the evidence is stronger or your starting belief was weaker.

name: A/B Testing
summary: Shows two versions to randomly split visitors, then asks whether the gap in results is bigger than luck alone would make. Stopping at the first win breaks the answer.
simple: An A/B test is a fair race between two versions of something. A shop wants to know whether a green Buy button sells more than its blue one. So each visitor is shown one of the two, chosen by a coin flip. After a while the shop counts. Say 10 in every 100 bought with blue, and 12 in every 100 bought with green. Is green better? Maybe. But two groups of people never behave exactly alike, even when they see the very same page. Some gap always appears by luck. So the test asks one question. If the buttons were really the same, how often would luck alone make a gap this big? If the answer is "hardly ever", the shop trusts the gap. If the answer is "quite often", it has learned nothing yet and needs more visitors. One rule is easy to break. Decide how many visitors to wait for before you start, and then wait. If you keep checking and stop the moment green is ahead, luck will fool you far more often.

analogy.title: A twitchy kitchen scale
analogy.text: You want to know whether two bags of flour weigh the same, but your scale is twitchy: weigh the same bag twice and it reads a little differently each time. One reading of each bag settles nothing. So you first learn how much the scale twitches, and then ask whether the two bags differ by clearly more than a twitch. An A/B test does this with people in place of flour. The twitch is the luck of who happened to visit. The test works out how big that twitch is for the number of visitors you had, and it calls a difference real only when the gap is about twice the twitch or more.
analogy.limits: You can weigh the same bag again, but you cannot show the same visitor both pages as if for the first time. The test has to compare two different groups and rely on chance to make them alike. A scale twitches by the same amount every day, while visitors change with the hour, the weekday and the season. And a scale tells you how much heavier a bag is, whereas the test on its own says only whether a difference probably exists, not whether it is large enough to matter.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: A shop shows its current checkout page (A) to 200 visitors and a new one (B) to another 200, with chance deciding who sees which. 30 of the A visitors buy and 50 of the B visitors buy. Is B really better, or would two identical pages often differ by this much?
whatFollows.takeaway: A gap between two versions means something only when it is clearly bigger than luck would make it, and only if you chose when to stop before you looked.

name: Exponential Smoothing
summary: Forecasts the next value of a series from a running estimate in which recent figures count most. Extra terms follow a trend and a repeating season.
simple: Exponential smoothing is a way to estimate next month's number from the months before. Picture a bakery deciding how many loaves to bake. Last month it sold 120. In the months before that it sold about 100. Which number should it trust? The newest one is the freshest news, but it might be a fluke. The older ones are steadier, but things may have changed since. Exponential smoothing takes a middle path. It keeps one running estimate. Each month it compares the estimate with what really happened, and moves the estimate part of the way toward the real figure. A small move ignores flukes but is slow to notice a real change. A big move reacts fast but gets pushed around by every odd month. Recent months end up counting most, and older months fade bit by bit. Two add-ons make it more useful. One keeps track of whether sales are climbing or falling. The other remembers which months of the year are always busy, like December in a toy shop.

analogy.title: Your opinion of a restaurant
analogy.text: You've eaten at a restaurant many times and have a settled opinion of it. Tonight, the meal is unusually bad. You don't decide the restaurant is terrible, but you don't ignore the experience either. Your opinion drops a little. If the next few meals are bad too, your opinion keeps falling until it reflects what the kitchen is serving now. Older meals still influence your view, but less and less as time passes. Exponential smoothing treats demand in much the same way. It keeps a running estimate and nudges it towards each new figure, while the influence of older figures gradually fades.
analogy.limits:
Your opinion changes by instinct. Exponential smoothing changes its estimate by a precise fraction, controlled by a setting called the smoothing weight. A small weight makes the estimate steadier but slower to react; a large one makes it quicker to react but more sensitive to unusual results. The best setting depends on the data and can be found by testing different values and measuring how well they forecast.

You might also know why tonight's meal was bad: perhaps the usual chef was away. The method knows nothing about the reasons behind the numbers. It cannot tell whether a poor result is a one-off or the start of a lasting change until later observations provide more evidence.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: A café wants to forecast how many cakes it will sell next month. In the last four months it sold 100, 110, 104 and 120. It uses simple smoothing with a weight of one half: each month the estimate moves halfway from where it was toward what was actually sold.
whatFollows.takeaway: Keep a running estimate, move it part of the way toward each new figure, and add a trend and a seasonal pattern when the history shows them.

name: Reservoir Sampling
summary: Keeps a uniform random sample of k items from a stream of unknown length, in one pass and with memory for only k items.
simple: Reservoir sampling picks a fair random handful from a stream of things when you do not know how long the stream will be. Imagine watching a parade with room in your notebook for only three names. Marchers pass one at a time, and nobody will tell you how many are coming. You want every marcher to have the same chance of ending up in your notebook. Writing down the first three would be unfair to everyone after them. Here is the trick. Write down the first three. When the fourth marcher passes, give them a three in four chance of replacing a name chosen at random from your notebook. Give the fifth marcher a three in five chance, the sixth a three in six chance, and so on. Later marchers are less likely to get in. But earlier names have faced more chances of being pushed out. The two effects balance exactly. Whenever the parade ends, every marcher has had the same chance.

analogy.title: Choosing one song from the radio
analogy.text: You decide to remember one song from tonight's radio show, chosen fairly, without knowing how many songs will play. Remember the first song. When the second plays, flip a coin to decide whether to switch to it. When the third plays, switch with a chance of one in three. For the tenth song, one in ten. At whatever moment the show ends, each song that played has had the same chance of being the one you remember.
analogy.limits: This is the case of a sample of one. Keeping several items needs the extra step of choosing which held item to replace. A person also cannot produce honest one-in-ten chances in their head, while a program uses a random number generator. And a fair chance is not the same as a representative result: a sample of one song says little about the whole show.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Keep a sample of 2 from a stream of items numbered 1, 2, 3 and so on in the order they arrive. The reservoir has two slots. For each item after the second, draw a random whole number between 1 and the item's position. If the number is 1 or 2, the new item replaces the item in that slot. Otherwise the new item is passed over.
whatFollows.takeaway: Keep the first k items, then let the i-th item replace a random one of them with chance k in i, and the sample stays fair however long the stream runs.

name: Metropolis-Hastings
summary: Draws samples from a distribution known only up to a constant by a random walk that accepts or rejects each proposed move according to a ratio of densities.
simple: Metropolis-Hastings is a way to explore a landscape in proportion to its height, when you can only measure the height where you stand. Imagine a hiker wandering through hills in fog. She wants to spend most of her time on high ground, and exactly twice as long at places that are twice as high. She has an altimeter but no map. So she follows a simple rule. Pick a random spot nearby and check its height. If it is higher, go there. If it is lower, go there only sometimes: half the time if it is half as high, one time in ten if it is a tenth as high. Otherwise stay put, and write down the place where she is standing once more. Keep a list of everywhere she stood. Over a long walk, that list traces the shape of the whole landscape. Scientists use this to study things they can score but cannot list in full, such as every arrangement of the atoms in a liquid, or every explanation that fits a set of measurements.

analogy.title: A politician touring a chain of islands
analogy.text: A politician wants to spend time on each island of a long chain in proportion to its population, but has no list of populations. Each day they consider moving to a randomly chosen neighbouring island and ask the mayors for the two populations. If the neighbour is larger, they go. If it is smaller, they go with probability equal to the ratio of the populations, and otherwise stay another day. After many days, the number of days spent on each island is proportional to its population.
analogy.limits: The islands are few and in a line. Real problems have a continuum of positions in many dimensions, where choosing a good size and direction for the proposed move is the hard part. The story also hides two facts. Successive days are not independent: where the politician is today depends on yesterday, so a week of days is worth far less than seven independent draws. And if two groups of islands are separated by a long stretch of empty ones, the politician may never cross, and nothing in the daily record would reveal that half the population was missed.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: A curve has two bumps: a smaller one centred at −2, where its height is 0.30, and a larger one centred at 2, where its height is 0.70. A walker starts at −2 and takes four steps. Each step comes with a proposed position, the height of the curve there, and a random number between 0 and 1 to settle the uncertain cases. The rule: divide the height at the proposed position by the height at the current position. If the random number is smaller than the result, move. Otherwise stay. Either way, write down where the walker now stands.
whatFollows.takeaway: Wander at random, always accept a move to somewhere more probable, accept a move to somewhere less probable only in proportion to how much less, and the places you visit become samples of the distribution.

name: Kalman Filter
summary: Tracks a changing quantity from noisy measurements by alternating a prediction from a motion model with a correction weighted by how reliable each source is.
simple: A Kalman filter keeps track of something that moves when your measurements of it are shaky. Think of following a friend's car on a phone map. The dot jumps around, because satellite positioning is never exact. But you know something else as well: a car on a road moves smoothly. A second ago it was there, driving that way at that speed, so now it should be about here. The filter blends these two sources. First it predicts where the car should be now. Then it looks at the new measurement and moves its guess part of the way toward it. How far? That depends on which source deserves more trust. If the measurements are poor, it leans on the prediction. If the prediction is doubtful, it leans on the measurement. It also keeps a running score of how unsure it is, and updates that score at every step. The result is a steadier and more accurate track than the raw measurements give.

analogy.title: A navigator with a compass and a glimpse of the coast
analogy.text: A ship's navigator without satellite positioning keeps a running estimate of the ship's position from its speed and heading. This is dead reckoning, and its error grows with every hour. Now and then the navigator sights a lighthouse and gets a position fix, which has its own error. A good navigator does not jump to the fix or ignore it, but moves the plotted position toward it by an amount that depends on how much each is trusted. After hours of dead reckoning, a fix counts for a lot. Just after a good fix, the next rough sighting counts for little.
analogy.limits: A navigator weighs things by judgement. The filter uses exact formulas that are only as good as the noise levels it is given. Tell it the sensor is better than it really is and it will follow the noise. The formulas also assume that errors are bell-shaped and that the motion follows a linear rule. A navigator can reason that the ship cannot be on land. The basic filter cannot represent a fact like that.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: A toy train moves along a track about 0.5 metres every second. A sensor reports its position, but the readings are noisy. The filter keeps two numbers: its estimate of the position, and a doubt score, called the variance, that says how unsure it is. The sensor's readings have a variance of 4. Each second of travel adds 1 to the filter's variance, because the train's speed wobbles. The filter starts with the estimate 0 and a variance of 3.
whatFollows.takeaway: Predict where the thing should be, look at where the sensor says it is, and settle in between, closer to whichever you have more reason to trust.

name: Particle Filter
summary: Tracks a hidden, changing quantity with a cloud of weighted guesses: move each guess, weigh it against the measurement, resample. Copes with beliefs that have several humps.
simple: A particle filter keeps track of something it cannot see directly by making many guesses at once. Picture a robot in a long hallway that has lost its place. It could be in several spots, so the filter scatters a few hundred guesses along the hallway. Each guess is called a particle, and each one says, "maybe the robot is here". Then three things happen, again and again. First, when the robot drives forward, every guess is moved forward too, with a small random nudge because wheels slip. Second, the robot's sensor takes a reading and each guess is scored. A guess that would have produced that reading scores high. A guess that would not scores low. Third, the filter makes a fresh set of guesses by copying the high scorers and dropping the low ones. After a few rounds the guesses crowd around the place where the robot really is. Because the guesses can sit in several places at once, the filter can stay undecided between two spots until the readings settle the matter.

analogy.title: A search party with one radio
analogy.text: A hiker is lost on a moor. Searchers spread out over every place she might be. Then a report comes over the radio: her phone was heard about two kilometres from the mast. Searchers standing about two kilometres from the mast are in promising places. Searchers anywhere else are wasting their time, so they walk over and join the promising ones. As the hiker moves, the searchers drift the way she is likely to drift. With each new report the party thins out in the wrong places and thickens in the right ones.
analogy.limits: Real searchers can look around, think and change the plan. A particle does nothing but hold a position. Real searchers who find nothing widen the search, while the basic filter can only copy the particles it already has: if none of them is near the truth, no amount of copying will put one there. And the filter moves its people by exact proportions computed from the sensor's error, where a search leader goes by judgement.
