whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: A robot is in a hallway with a beacon at position 0. Positions are in metres: negative numbers are left of the beacon and positive numbers are right of it. The sensor reports the distance to the beacon, typically wrong by about 1 m, and it cannot tell left from right. The filter holds four guesses, called particles, at −5, −4, 4 and 6. Each carries a quarter of the belief: that share is its weight. For this sensor, a particle whose expected reading misses the real reading by 1 m scores 0.61, and one that misses by 2 m scores 0.14. To keep the arithmetic short, the small random nudges of the full method are left out here.
whatFollows.takeaway: Scatter many guesses, move them as the thing moves, and after every reading keep copies of the guesses that fit it: the survivors show where the thing is.

name: Rapidly-Exploring Random Tree (RRT)
summary: Plans a collision-free path by growing a tree from the start toward random points, one short obstacle-checked branch at a time, until a branch reaches the goal.
simple: A rapidly-exploring random tree, or RRT, finds a way for a robot to get from one place to another without bumping into things. It works a little like a plant growing through a garden full of rocks. The plant starts as a single shoot at the robot's starting point. Again and again, the planner picks a random spot somewhere on the map. It finds the part of the plant that is closest to that spot and grows a short new twig from there toward it. If the twig would poke through a rock, it is thrown away. Otherwise it stays. Random spots are scattered all over the map, so the plant is pulled outward in every direction and soon reaches into every open area. When a twig comes close enough to the goal, the planner follows the plant back from that twig to the root. That chain of twigs is a route the robot can follow. The route is usually crooked. It is the first one found, not the shortest.

analogy.title: Explorers and a dispatcher
analogy.text: A team is exploring an unmapped island from a base camp. A dispatcher, who cannot see the terrain, keeps calling out random map coordinates. Each time, the camp nearest to those coordinates sends a scout a short walk in that direction. If the way is clear, the scout sets up a new camp there, linked by a trail to the one they left. If a cliff is in the way, the scout turns back. Coordinates far from any camp are always answered by a camp on the edge of the explored area, so the camps spread quickly across the whole island. When a camp is set up next to the destination, the trail back to base is the route.
analogy.limits: Real scouts would learn from a cliff and walk around it. The algorithm learns nothing from a failed branch and may try the same wall many times. A real robot's position is often a list of joint angles and not a place on a map, and its obstacles in that space are invisible shapes known only through a yes-or-no collision test. And scouts can walk in any direction, while a car cannot move sideways: for such robots, moving toward the target needs more than a straight line.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: A robot at (1, 1) must get around a wall. The wall is a thin vertical strip between x = 3 and x = 3.4, reaching from the bottom of the map up to y = 5.5. The tree starts as the single point (1, 1), and each new branch may be at most 1 long. Four random targets arrive in turn.
whatFollows.takeaway: Grow a tree from the start by pulling its nearest point a short, obstacle-checked step toward one random spot after another, and it will spread through the open space until it touches the goal.

name: Run-Length Encoding
summary: Replaces each run of a repeated symbol with a count and the symbol. Shrinks data with long runs and makes data without runs larger.
simple: Run-length encoding is a way to write repeated things in less space. Suppose you are reading a row of floor tiles aloud to a friend: white, white, white, white, white, white, black, black. You would soon stop naming each tile. You would say "six white, then two black" instead. That is the whole idea. A run is a stretch of the same thing repeated, with nothing else in between. Run-length encoding replaces every run with two pieces of information: how many, and of what. Your friend can rebuild the row exactly, tile for tile, so nothing is lost. This saves a lot of space when the data has long runs, like a drawing with large areas of one colour. It does not help with ordinary writing, where a letter is rarely followed by the same letter. There it makes things longer, because every single letter now needs its own count.

analogy.title: A knitting pattern
analogy.text: A knitting pattern does not list every stitch. It says "knit 6, purl 2, knit 6". The knitter reads a count and a kind of stitch, and produces exactly the row the designer meant. Run-length encoding writes data the same way: a count, then the thing to repeat.
analogy.limits: A designer chooses rows with long repeats. Data does not cooperate like that. A row that switched between knit and purl on every stitch would be longer as a pattern than as a plain list, and that is exactly what happens to ordinary text. The picture also hides a cost. A person reads "6" without thinking about the room it takes, but in a file the count occupies space of its own: 8 bits for every run in this lesson.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Encode the ten letters AAAABBBCCD. A bit is a single 0 or 1, the smallest unit of computer storage. In this lesson every letter of the input takes 8 bits, so the input is 80 bits. Every pair in the output takes 16 bits: 8 for the count and 8 for the letter.
whatFollows.takeaway: Instead of repeating a symbol, say how many times it repeats, and expect this to pay off only when the repeats are long.

name: Huffman Coding
summary: Builds the best symbol-by-symbol code for a text by repeatedly joining the two rarest symbols into a tree, so common symbols get short codes.
simple: Huffman coding is a way to write a message using as few 0s and 1s as possible. A computer stores every letter as a pattern of 0s and 1s, and normally every letter gets a pattern of the same length. That is wasteful, because some letters turn up far more often than others. In English, e is everywhere and z is rare. Huffman coding gives short patterns to the common letters and longer patterns to the rare ones. Morse code does something similar: the letter e is a single dot. There is one more requirement. The patterns must be chosen so that the message can be read back without any gaps between letters. For that, no pattern may be the beginning of another pattern. Huffman coding finds such a set by tying the two rarest letters together, treating the pair as one, and repeating until everything is joined into a single tree. For that message, no other set of patterns of this kind is shorter.

analogy.title: Morse code, with the gaps removed
analogy.text: Morse code gives the commonest English letters the shortest signals: E is one dot and T is one dash, while Q is dash dash dot dash. A telegraph operator therefore sends fewer signals for ordinary text than a code with equal-length letters would need. Huffman coding follows the same principle, short for common and long for rare, and works out the best lengths from actual counts.
analogy.limits: Morse code cannot be read as an unbroken stream. One dot is E, and it is also the start of A (dot dash), so the operator must leave a silence between letters. That silence is a third signal. A Huffman code needs no silences, because no code is the beginning of another. Morse code was also fixed once for all English text, while a Huffman code is computed for one particular set of counts and is only the best code for those counts.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Encode the nine letters ABACABADA. A bit is a single 0 or 1. Start by counting: A appears 5 times, B appears 2 times, C once and D once. A plain code for four letters gives each one 2 bits, which makes 18 bits in total.
whatFollows.takeaway: Give common symbols short codes and rare symbols long ones, by joining the two rarest again and again until one tree is left.

name: LZ77 Compression
summary: Replaces a repeated stretch of text with a pointer back to an earlier copy: how far back to go and how many symbols to copy.
simple: LZ77 is a way to make a text shorter by not writing the same thing twice. Think about how people write. Words and phrases come back again and again. When you copy out a long song, you do not write the chorus every time. You write "repeat chorus". LZ77 does this automatically, for any kind of repeat. It reads the text from start to finish. At each point it looks back over the last stretch it has read and asks: have I seen what comes next before? If so, it does not write those letters again. It writes a short note instead: go back this far, and copy this many letters. If not, it writes the letter as it is. Someone holding the notes can rebuild the whole text, because every note points to something already rebuilt. The more a text repeats itself, the shorter it gets. A text with no repeats gets longer, because each note takes up room too.

analogy.title: A song sheet that says "repeat chorus"
analogy.text: A printed song does not spell out the chorus after every verse. It prints the chorus once and afterwards writes "repeat chorus". The singer looks back up the page, finds the words and sings them again. LZ77 writes that kind of instruction for every repeat it can find: look back this far, and copy this much.
analogy.limits: A songwriter knows where the chorus is and gives it a name. LZ77 has no names. It can only point backwards by distance, and only as far as its window reaches, so a phrase that returns after a long gap is not found. It also matches exact symbols only: a chorus with one changed word is copied up to the change and no further. And every instruction costs bits, so copying one or two letters usually costs more than writing them out.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Encode the nine letters ABABCABAB. The search window is the last 16 letters read and the look-ahead buffer is the next 8. A bit is a single 0 or 1. Each input letter takes 8 bits, so the input is 72 bits. Each triple (how far back, how many to copy, next letter) takes 15 bits here: 4 for the distance, 3 for the count and 8 for the letter.
whatFollows.takeaway: When something you are about to write has appeared recently, point back to it and say how much to copy instead of writing it again.

name: Byte-Pair Encoding
summary: Builds a vocabulary of word pieces by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair of tokens in a text, then splits new text by replaying the same merges.
simple: Byte-pair encoding is a way to chop text into pieces that a computer can treat as single units. Whole words make poor pieces. There are too many of them, and new ones keep turning up. Single letters make poor pieces too. There are only a few, but every text becomes a very long string of them. Byte-pair encoding finds pieces in between. It starts with the text split into single letters. Then it looks for the two neighbouring pieces that occur together most often, such as t next to h, and glues them into one new piece, th. It writes that rule down and looks again. After many rounds the common words have become single pieces. Rarer words are built from a few familiar chunks, the way slowest is slow plus est. Any new word can then be split by replaying the same rules in the same order. The pieces are called tokens. Language models, including the ones behind chatbots, read and write text as tokens made in this way or a similar one.

analogy.title: Inventing shorthand as you go
analogy.text: Someone copying out a long document by hand notices that they keep writing the same two marks side by side. They invent one new mark for the pair and note it in a legend at the top of the page: "this mark means t then h". Later they notice the new mark often sits next to e, so they invent another mark for that, defined in terms of the first. The legend grows one line at a time, and each line may use marks defined above it. Anyone holding the legend can copy out new documents in the same shorthand, and can expand the shorthand back into the original letters.
analogy.limits: A person would invent shorthand for units that mean something. Byte-pair encoding follows the counts wherever they lead, so its pieces can cut across meaning. A person might also revise the legend later. Here a rule, once made, is never reconsidered, and the legend depends entirely on the one text it was built from. And when two pairs are equally common a person would use judgment, while the method needs a fixed tie rule so that everyone who repeats the work gets the same legend.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Learn two merges from the three-word text "ha ha hat", then use them to split the word "aha". A token is one piece of text that is treated as a unit. At the start every letter is its own token, and a marker, written _, is added at the end of each word. So the text starts as h a _ and h a _ and h a t _, which is 10 tokens.
whatFollows.takeaway: Keep gluing together the two neighbouring pieces that occur most often, remember the order you did it in, and replay those steps to split any new text.

name: Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange
summary: Two parties agree on a shared secret over a public channel using modular powers. Shown with toy numbers that are insecure and for learning only.
simple: Diffie-Hellman key exchange lets two people agree on a secret number while everyone else is listening. That sounds impossible. If Alice and Bob have never met, and a stranger hears every word they say, how can they end up sharing a secret? The answer is a kind of arithmetic that is easy to do and very hard to undo. Alice and Bob each pick a private number and keep it to themselves. Each one scrambles a public starting number using their private number, and sends the result. Then each scrambles what they received, using their own private number again. Both arrive at the same final number. The listener saw the two scrambled results, but cannot work backwards to either private number, so cannot reach the final one. That final number becomes the key that locks the rest of the conversation. On this page the numbers are tiny so that you can follow every step. Numbers this small are easy to crack. They are for learning only and protect nothing.

analogy.title: Mixing paint in public
analogy.text: Alice and Bob agree, in the open, on a common paint colour, say yellow. Each secretly chooses a private colour. Each mixes their private colour into some yellow and sends the mixture to the other, where anyone can see it. Then each stirs their own private colour into the mixture they received. Both now hold yellow plus Alice's colour plus Bob's colour, the same final shade. A spy saw yellow and the two mixtures. Separating a mixture back into its ingredients is impractical, and without one of the private colours she cannot make the final shade.
analogy.limits: Paint is only a picture of "easy to do, hard to undo". Un-mixing paint is hard for physical reasons. Undoing the arithmetic is hard only as far as anyone knows: for large, well-chosen numbers no fast method has been found, but nobody has proved that none exists, and a large quantum computer could do it. With small numbers, like the ones on this page, it is easy. The picture also says nothing about who you are mixing with. If someone sits in the middle and swaps the tins, Alice and Bob each end up sharing a colour with that person instead of with each other. The real protocol has exactly this weakness unless the messages are also signed.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Alice and Bob agree in public on the prime 23 and the base 5. All arithmetic is done "mod 23": after multiplying, divide by 23 and keep only the remainder. Alice secretly picks 3 and Bob secretly picks 6. These numbers are far too small to be safe. They are only for following the steps.
whatFollows.takeaway: Each side mixes a private number into a public one, swaps the results and mixes again, so both reach the same secret and it never has to travel.

name: RSA
summary: Public-key encryption from two secret primes: anyone can encrypt with (n, e), only the holder of d can decrypt. Shown as insecure textbook RSA with toy primes.
simple: RSA is a way to send a secret to someone you have never met, without agreeing on a password first. Picture a padlock that anyone can snap shut but only one key can open. The receiver hands out open padlocks to everybody and keeps the key at home. To send a secret, you put it in a box, snap a padlock on it and post it. Not even you can open it again. Only the receiver can. RSA builds this padlock out of numbers. The receiver secretly picks two prime numbers, which are numbers such as 7 or 13 that nothing divides evenly except 1 and themselves. Multiplying the two primes gives a number that is made public. It acts as the padlock. The primes themselves stay secret and act as the key. Multiplying two primes is quick. Finding them again from the answer is extremely slow when the primes are hundreds of digits long. On this page the primes are tiny, so that you can follow every step. Numbers this small can be cracked at once. They are for learning only, and you should never build your own version to protect anything real.

analogy.title: An open padlock that anyone can snap shut
analogy.text: The receiver makes a padlock and a key, keeps the key, and gives copies of the open padlock to anyone who asks. A sender puts a message in a box and snaps the padlock shut. From that moment nobody can open the box, including the sender, except the person with the key. The padlock can be handed around freely because closing it teaches you nothing about how to open it.
analogy.limits: A steel padlock is opened by cutting it. The RSA padlock is opened by arithmetic: anyone who can split the public number into its two primes can make the key. Nobody has proved that this splitting must be slow, and a large enough quantum computer could do it quickly. A padlock also behaves the same way every time, and for a padlock that is fine. For RSA it is a weakness: locking the same message twice gives the same result, so a spy who can guess the message can lock her guess and compare. Real systems mix random padding into the message before locking it. The picture also leaves out how a sender knows the padlock really belongs to the receiver, which needs certificates.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: The receiver picks the primes 3 and 11. Their product is 33, which is made public. From the primes the receiver computes (3 − 1) × (11 − 1) = 20, and keeps it secret. The public exponent is 3, which shares no factor with 20. The private exponent is 7, because 3 × 7 = 21, which is one more than 20. "Mod 33" means: divide by 33 and keep the remainder. These numbers are far too small to be safe and are only for following the steps. The message is the number 2.
whatFollows.takeaway: Multiplying two large primes is easy and undoing it is hard, so the product can be a public lock while the primes stay the private key.

name: Bresenham's Line Algorithm
summary: Draws a straight line on a pixel grid by stepping one pixel at a time and tracking the drift from the true line with whole-number additions only.
simple: A screen is a grid of tiny squares called pixels. Each pixel is either lit or dark. So how do you draw a slanted line? You cannot light half a pixel. You have to choose whole pixels that sit as close to the true line as they can. Bresenham's algorithm chooses them one at a time. It walks from one end of the line to the other, one column per step. At each step there are only two choices: stay in the same row, or move over by one row. To decide, it keeps one running number. That number says how far the chosen pixels have drifted from the true line. When the drift passes half a pixel, the walk moves over a row and the number drops back. The number is always a whole number, with no fractions. So the method only needs to add, subtract and compare, which even a very basic computer chip does quickly.

analogy.title: Stacking blocks beside a ramp
analogy.text: Picture a long, gentle ramp, and a supply of square blocks that you stack beside it so the block tops follow the ramp as closely as blocks can. Walk along the ramp one block-width at a time. At each stop, look at the gap between the ramp and the top of your stack. If the ramp has climbed more than half a block above the stack, add one block. Otherwise leave the stack alone. You never measure the ramp from the ground again. You only keep track of the gap, and the gap changes by the same amount at every stop.
analogy.limits: A person would measure the gap with a ruler and get fractions. The algorithm avoids that: it scales everything by a fixed whole number first, so the quantity it tracks is always a whole number, and it compares against zero instead of against half a block. The ramp also only climbs gently to the right. Real lines can head in any direction, including steeper than 45 degrees, where the algorithm must walk row by row instead of column by column. And a pixel is a small square of light, so a drawn line still looks like a staircase when you look closely.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Draw a line from pixel (0, 0) to pixel (5, 2). It goes 5 pixels across and 2 up, so step one column at a time. Keep one whole number called the error term. It starts at 2 × 2 − 5 = −1: twice the rise, minus the run. Before each step, check it. If it is above zero, go up a row and subtract 10, which is twice the run. Then always add 4, which is twice the rise.
whatFollows.takeaway: Take one step per pixel along the line's longer direction, and step sideways whenever a running whole-number tally says the true line has drifted more than half a pixel.

name: Graham Scan
summary: Finds the convex hull of points in the plane: sort them by angle around the lowest point, then sweep once, discarding every point that would make a right turn.
simple: Hammer some nails into a board. Now stretch a rubber band around all of them and let go. It snaps tight against the outermost nails and ignores the rest. That outline is called the convex hull. Convex means it has no dents. A computer has no rubber band, so it needs a method. Graham scan starts at the lowest nail, which must be on the outline. It then visits the other nails in order, sweeping around like a clock hand running backwards. It joins each nail to the one before, as if drawing the outline. After each new nail it checks the last corner it drew. If the path bends left there, fine. If it bends right, that corner is a dent, so the nail there cannot be on the outline. The nail is dropped, and the corner before it is checked again. When the sweep ends, the nails still kept are the corners of the rubber band's shape.

analogy.title: A rubber band around nails
analogy.text: Nails stand in a board, one for each point. Stretch a rubber band wide enough to surround them all and let go. It pulls in until it is stopped by the outermost nails, and it ends up as a polygon with straight sides and no dents. The nails it bends around are the corners of the convex hull. Nails in the middle never touch it.
analogy.limits: The band finds the whole outline at once, by physics. A computer has only a list of coordinates and must examine points a few at a time, which is why the sort and the stack are needed. A real band also rests against nails that happen to stand along a straight side, between two corners. This lesson's algorithm reports only the corners and leaves those out. Real nails have thickness and a real band has stretch; points have neither. And the picture is flat. In three dimensions the hull is more like shrink-wrap pulled over the points, and this scan does not carry over, because there is no single order in which to sweep around.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Five nails stand at (0, 0), (4, 1), (3, 2), (4, 4) and (1, 3). The lowest is (0, 0), so start there. Seen from it, sweeping counter-clockwise from the right, the others come in the order (4, 1), (3, 2), (4, 4), (1, 3). Keep a pile of the points that currently look like corners. This pile is called a stack: you only ever add to its top or remove from its top.
whatFollows.takeaway: Start at the lowest point, sweep around the others in order, and throw away any point where the outline would bend to the right.

name: Consistent Hashing
summary: Assigns keys to servers by position on a ring, so that adding or removing one server moves only the keys next to it instead of nearly all of them.
simple: Big websites keep their data on many computers, called servers. To fetch a piece of data, a program must know which server holds it. A simple rule is to number the servers and do a little arithmetic on the data's name. That rule has a flaw. Add or remove one server, and almost every piece of data is suddenly assigned somewhere else. Nearly everything would have to be copied to a new home. Consistent hashing avoids this. Imagine a circle, like a clock face. Each server is given a spot on the circle. Each piece of data is given a spot too. The data belongs to the first server you meet when you walk clockwise from its spot. Now add a new server. It takes over only the stretch of circle just behind it. The data on that stretch moves to the new server. Everything else stays exactly where it was.

analogy.title: Stops on a circular bus route
analogy.text: A road runs in a ring round a town, with houses all along it and a handful of bus stops. Everybody walks clockwise along the road to the first stop they come to. If the town builds a new stop, only the households between the previous stop and the new one change their habits: they now reach the new stop first. If a stop closes, only its own passengers are affected. They walk on to the next one. Nobody else in town notices.
analogy.limits: Houses and bus stops stand where they do for reasons. On a hash ring every position is a scrambled number with no meaning, and that scrambling is what spreads the keys evenly. Nobody walks, either: finding the next server is a quick search in a sorted list of positions. The picture also leaves out two things real systems add. Each server is given many positions, not one, so that the stretches even out. And each item is usually stored on several servers in a row, so that losing one server loses no data.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Picture a ring with positions numbered 0 to 99, where 99 is followed by 0 again. Three servers have been given positions: A at 10, B at 40 and C at 75. Six keys have positions 7, 22, 38, 51, 64 and 93. A key belongs to the first server at or after its position, going upward and wrapping round past 99.
whatFollows.takeaway: Put servers and keys on a circle and give each key to the next server clockwise; then adding or removing a server only disturbs the keys right beside it.

name: Grover's Search
summary: A quantum algorithm that finds one marked item among N with about √N uses of the test that recognizes it, where any classical search needs about N/2.
simple: Suppose you have a huge pile of keys and one lock. Only one key fits, and the only way to find out is to try a key in the lock. An ordinary computer tries keys one at a time. On average it gets through half the pile. Grover's search is a method for a quantum computer that needs far fewer tries: for a million keys, about eight hundred. It does not test every key at the same moment. The state of a quantum computer is described by a list of numbers, one for each key, called amplitudes. Nobody can read these numbers directly. When you look at the machine you see just one key, and a key with a bigger number is more likely to be the one you see. Each use of the lock test, followed by one fixed adjustment, makes the right key's number grow and the others shrink. After the right number of rounds, looking gives the right key almost every time. Quantum computers big enough to do this for a useful problem do not exist yet. This page uses an ordinary computer to work out the same numbers.

analogy.title: Turning a dial in equal clicks
analogy.text: Picture a dial with a pointer. Straight up means "certain to see the right answer". Flat means "certain to see a wrong one". At the start the pointer is almost flat, because the right answer is one among many. Each round of the algorithm turns the pointer upward by the same small angle. After enough rounds it points nearly straight up, and that is the moment to look. Keep turning and it swings past the top and back down, so extra rounds make things worse.
analogy.limits: There is no pointer inside the machine. The dial is a summary of a long list of amplitudes, and the turning comes from two operations that make some amplitudes add up and others cancel. Ordinary chances never cancel each other like that, which is why no everyday object behaves this way. You also cannot watch the dial. Looking at a quantum computer gives one answer and destroys the state, so the number of rounds has to be worked out beforehand. And the dial says nothing about cost. Each click needs the test to be built as a quantum circuit and run without errors, which is the hard part in practice.

whatFollows.workedExampleSetup: Four boxes are numbered 0, 1, 2 and 3, and box 2 is the one we are looking for. Each box has a number attached, called its amplitude. The chance of seeing a box when you look is its amplitude multiplied by itself. Start with every amplitude at 0.5, so each box has a chance of 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25, one in four.
whatFollows.takeaway: Grover's search does not check every answer at once: it uses about the square root of N checks to make the right answer the one a measurement almost surely shows.
